# Front Cover

The volume is bound in a dark brown <term>morocco leather</term><note>Morocco is a high-quality, fine-grained leather traditionally made from goatskin, prized for its durability and beauty.</note> with a fine, pebbled texture that has aged to a deep, rich tone. 

->**Binding Decoration**<-

In the center of the cover is a small, decorative <term>gilt</term><note>Gilt refers to the application of thin gold leaf to the leather through a heated brass tool.</note> stamp of a <term>wheatsheaf</term><note>In heraldry, a wheatsheaf is known as a "garb" and often symbolizes abundance or agricultural heritage.</note>. 

The spine on the left edge shows five distinct <term>raised bands</term><note>These horizontal ridges indicate where the cords used to sew the book's sections together are located under the leather, a hallmark of traditional hand-binding.</note>, characteristic of early modern bookbinding techniques.

# THE ANTIPODES <note>original: "ANTIPODES". While literally meaning those on the opposite side of the globe, the author uses this to address people who might see the world differently than the corrupt society he is satirizing.</note>

->*Greetings to you,*<-
->*good, simple, and wise men.*<- <note>original: "Viri boni, simplices & cordati". These adjectives describe the ideal reader: virtuous, without deceit, and possessing a sound heart or intellect.</note>

I send to you, my best friends, an image of our hemisphere—drawn not with the brush of Apelles <note>Apelles was the most famous painter of ancient Greece, known for his perfect technique. The author is saying his work is a rough sketch, not a masterpiece.</note> but with a random piece of charcoal. There is no hope of any small profit <note>original: "Lucelli", a diminutive of "lucrum" meaning small gain or "filthy lucre."</note> from you, except for the desire to compare this work with your own circumstances. Come then, if you have anything among you equally or even less absurd, share it, since we have both encountered the same very rough world <note>original: "globũ scabrosissimum". This refers to the Earth as a coarse, unpolished sphere, mirroring the "roughness" of human behavior.</note>. There is no literary style here except for frankness <term>parrhesia: a Greek term for "speaking truth to power" or "bold, uninhibited speech," often used by satirical philosophers like Menippus.</term>. There are no authors here other than eyes, ears, and touch. Modesty has restrained the flatterer; the Sun is my witness, whom I have entreated to be a messenger to you. Live well, and have compassion. Toward the North, at 50 degrees of polar elevation <note>A geographical coordinate. 50 degrees North passes through cities like Mainz, Prague, or Frankfurt, hinting at the author's real-world location.</note>.

*Even though in every age the pursuit of truth has been just as great as the hatred of it—the former never being restrained even amidst the most savage threats, and the latter never ceasing even in the clearest light—rarely, however, has the merit of both been equal among men. For since the actions of the worldly stage* <note>original: "mundanæ scenæ". In a legal sense, a "patrocinium" is the protection or advocacy provided by a patron.</note>, *perhaps invited by the happiness of the times or the favor of princes, scarcely indeed have they liberated truth—either sufficiently or for long—from the tyranny of opinions. Instead, having shown their effort in a praiseworthy cause, as soon as they realized the matter was as dangerous as it was most laborious, their mind*

# TO THE FAIR-MINDED READER.

*...considered it enough to have explained it with impunity. From this it follows that the labors of those most ingenious philosophers were in vain, by which they wished to have the heavens, the lands, the seas, and man himself recalled to and examined by the standard of truth and goodness. Great volumes were composed for this purpose, yet they always struggled against the vertigo* <note>original: "vertigine". In this context, it refers to a sense of dizziness or lack of stability in human reasoning.</note> *of the human brain, the slipperiness of changeable time, and the nobility of this machine of ours* <note>original: "machinæ huius noſtræ". This likely refers to the "world-machine" (the universe) or the human body as a complex divine creation.</note>, *until our Christ—Truth and Goodness itself and the salvation of the world—walking among us and calling out to the world in vain, openly showed us that there is no reason for us to hope for anything further from it, nor to expend our labors except in vain. He showed us, clearly, that this is a kingdom of darkness and of storms, where no matter what you attempt, "Ethiopians never turn white,"* <note>original: "æthiopes nūquam albeſcant". A common Latin proverb (Aethiopem lavare) meaning to labor at an impossible task or to try to change the unchangeable.</note> *and the blind cannot be delighted by the light. Yet, the world must still be rebuked so that when He is about to decree judgment concerning each individual at the Final Judgment, the conscience may be tormented by the memory of the truth it heard. From that time, when every good man has been buffeted by the hatred of Satan* <note>original: "Sathanæ odio". The author views the opposition to truth as a spiritual conflict.</note>, *he has sought to provide for his own people through the confession of truth; and for this one name alone he has always been mocked and accused, frequently [enriching] the fields of the Church with fi-* <meta>catchword: deli</meta>

<summary>The author argues that human philosophy failed to find absolute truth until Christ revealed the world to be a "kingdom of darkness" where effort is often futile. He frames the struggle for truth as a spiritual battle against the "hatred of Satan" that results in the persecution of the faithful.</summary>

<margin>B.</margin> And to you, my friend <note>original: "mi homo". A polite, somewhat familiar form of address.</note>.
<margin>A.</margin> I am going to entrust my son to you.
<margin>B.</margin> And I shall return him to you.
<margin>A.</margin> In what state?
<margin>B.</margin> Learned and successful.
<margin>A.</margin> These are magnificent promises, but I beg you, explain how this is done.
<margin>B.</margin> From me, he will learn how to persuade men of whatever he wishes, how to track down the truth everywhere, how to know all of Nature, how to study the heavens with precision, how to shape his life perfectly, how to govern citizens with wisdom, and how to have God as a familiar friend.
<margin>A.</margin> I am stunned.
<margin>B.</margin> Why so?
<margin>A.</margin> That you bestow such things on others while reserving none of them for yourself.
<margin>B.</margin> None?
<margin>A.</margin> None at all; for you have not persuaded me of this, nor do you speak the truth, nor do you have Nature as a friend, nor the heavens favoring you, nor a life respected by good men, nor obedient citizens, nor a merciful God.
<margin>B.</margin> Is this not an injustice?
<margin>A.</margin> On the contrary, it is a kindness, for I am judging you no more harshly than this: that you were intending to trade empty words for cold, hard cash <note>original: "verba daturus eras pro ære præsente". This is a Latin idiom for "selling air" or deceiving someone by offering worthless talk in exchange for immediate payment.</note>.
<margin>B.</margin> It ought to have been put to the test first.
<margin>A.</margin> If my boy were not a human being and my own son—whom I would be insane to let you use for a dangerous experiment, even if you paid for it yourself—I might agree.
<margin>B.</margin> Why then did you come here?
<margin>A.</margin> To see you in person, you who deceive so many fathers.
<margin>B.</margin> Do you call me an impostor?
<margin>A.</margin> Certainly so, for since [you make] no one bett-

...better, you immediately have others whom you may deceive. *B.* No one? *A.* Name someone. *B.* On the contrary, many. *A.* Just one. *B.* Bah, I am overwhelmed by the number. *A.* Spit out the first one that comes to mind <note>original: "qui primus in bucca" — literally "whoever is first in the mouth," an idiom for speaking the first thing that occurs to one.</note>. *B.* Should I be a plaything for you? *A.* Should I trust my son to you? *B.* Should I shape your blockhead? <note>original: "truncum" — literally a tree trunk or log; a common metaphor for a dull or stupid person who needs "carving" by a teacher.</note> *A.* Should I buy your nonsense? *B.* Should I be mixed up in your filth? *A.* Should I worship your rods? <note>A reference to the bundles of rods used by schoolmasters to administer corporal punishment.</note> *B.* Should I go without my pleasures? *A.* Should I spare my fists? *B.* And so, you will not entrust your son to me. *A.* Certainly not, even if he were a dog dearer than all the rest.

### 2. THE CALLING <note>original: "VOCATIO". In this context, it refers to the "divine call" or the formal process of being appointed to a church office.</note>.

*A.* Why are you sad? *B.* I have come from the inner sanctuaries <note>original: "adytis" — the most private or sacred parts of a temple; here likely referring to the administrative offices of the church hierarchy.</note>. *A.* What were you doing there? *B.* I was canvassing for the priesthood. *A.* A crime! You should have been called. *B.* Fool, as if I would want to wait another nine-year period. *A.* And so it is necessary to canvass? *B.* Nay, to buy it; for if I had the coins, I would not be grieving now. *A.* But what about the "calling" indeed? *B.* That is owed to those who have the right of primogeniture <note>The legal right of the firstborn son to inherit the entire family estate.</note> or inheritance. *A.* You speak obscurely. *B.* Thus it is fitting in the "mysteries" <note>A sarcastic reference to the secretive and often corrupt dealings of the church leadership.</note>. *A.* And so you place either a family name or silver beneath the sacred office? *B.* Such is the will of the times. *A.* And you buy the care of souls? *B.* We are forced to. *A.* Do you sell them? *B.* If the hope of the wool <note>original: "lanae" — a metaphor comparing the congregation to a flock of sheep; the speaker suggests he is interested in "shearing" them for money.</note> is worth more. *A.* Is there no conscience here? *B.* Poverty prevents it. *A.* Evidently, you are destined for priestly leisure in such numbers by your parents that you ought to be kept away from the Church, not prayed into it. **B.** And I am to believe I learned this from Machiavelli? 

**A.** Rather from the World, of which he was the most sagacious observer and most straightforward chronicler <note>original: "annotator"</note>. 

**B.** At the very least, let him perish, because there is so much evil in him. 

**A.** If that is what you wish, neither wood nor hearth would be enough to burn it all. Instead, commit the matter to God, to whom the universal malice of the World is known, and which He circumvents with the greatest wisdom. 

**B.** Will Machiavelli live on? 

**A.** He will live—if for no other reason, then certainly because he is the most open witness to human wickedness.

# APOSTASY.

...to me, too many people seem to judge religion too freely, feel for it too coldly, and decide upon it too unfairly.

*A.* You are mistaken to apply the name of the **Church** to this; for although it may possess less light at one time and more at another, it still shines for God and is not stained by the wickedness of earthly matters.

*B.* Are these not stains—that entire lands and such a vast flock of those who were set free should renounce **Christ**?

*A.* Yet the whole **World** has done this for a long time, and will continue to do so, unless you believe **Christ** is less offended by impiety than by errors.

*B.* Even among us?

*A.* Entirely. For to claim by Christian confession to be the most sincere of all and to agree with the scriptures <term>to the fingernail</term> <note>original: "ad unguem"—a phrase meaning "perfectly" or "down to the finest detail," like a sculptor checking a seam with a thumbnail</note>, yet to be no better in one's morals—what else is this but to shamefully mock **Christ**?

*B.* Mortals will never be without flaws.

*A.* Never indeed; but I ask you to consider within yourself what blasphemies, luxury, lusts, vanities, robberies, iniquities, pleasures, and deceptions are publicly tolerated among us, or even nearly approved. Since all these things have nothing at all in common with **Christ**, what does it matter which **religion** we belong to?

*B.* Are there not severe laws against criminals, and frequent examples of punishment?

*A.* For the weak, certainly; but the more powerful are "punished" with honors <note>original: "elogia"—here used ironically to mean that the powerful receive citations of merit or praise rather than actual sentences</note>.

*B.* But these men await **Christ** as their judge.

*A.* Precisely. You see then that our affairs—given such a poorly Christian administration of public life—must be left to **God** himself. He governs this age by His own will so that it might not lead the pious into ruin.

*B.* What, meanwhile, will be owed to those who champion the truth?

*A.* Their own praise, which would only then be complete if those same...

### 8. THE SALARY.

<margin>*A.*</margin> Can you bear one question?

*A.* What if the place is less suitable for the business <term>negotiationi</term> to which you are inclined?

# 10. THE BEGGAR.

*A.* May you have a good day. *B.* But it was never a bad one. *A.* May you become fortunate; why do you speak this way? *B.* Nor was I ever unfortunate at any time. *A.* Be happy <note>original: "Felix" — also translates to "blessed" or "lucky"</note>, for I do not understand your grand words. *B.* But I do not remember ever having been unhappy. *A.* May God save you; speak more clearly. *B.* Gladly. You were wishing for a "good day," but how can a day be "bad" which God sends? Whether I freeze, sweat, burn, thirst, or hunger, or if I am despised, I will praise God, whose will it is. Then you wished for me to become "fortunate": Is he not fortunate who is in agreement with God, and accepts all things from Him, whatever they may be, and expects everything from Him alone? Finally, you commanded me to be "happy": I am he who, through poverty and the lack of all things, emulates God <note>The speaker suggests that by stripping away worldly possessions, he achieves a state of self-sufficiency similar to the Divine</note>, reserving no will for myself, but depending instead on the Divine pleasure. *A.* What if that God of yours should cast you away? *B.* He cannot; I embrace Him with humble love and sublime faith, by which I am inseparably joined to God; wherever He is, there I shall be. I would rather be in hell with God than in heaven without Him <note>A famous expression of mystical devotion: the presence of God is more important than the physical location or the reward of paradise</note>. *A.* Where did you come from? *B.* From God; I live in God, and I return to God. *A.* Where did you find God? *B.* Where I left all creatures behind. *A.* Where is the seat of God? *B.* A pure heart and a ready will. *A.* Who are you? *B.* I am a King. *A.* Where is your kingdom? *B.* My soul; I conduct its rule—which was entrusted to me by God—in such a way that neither my external nor internal senses wander out of bounds. *A.* What rules of governing do you have? *B.* Silence, prayer, patience,

### 13. THE LATIN LANGUAGE.

**A.** I have always tolerated the ambition of the Latin language, though with difficulty; but that it exercises a tyranny over the Church <note>original: "in Ecclesiam tyrannidem agit"</note> is too much. **B.** You say "tyranny"? This is the language that alone has provided the Church with so many excellent and sacred writers that we can never be equal to returning the thanks due to it. **A.** I do not deny that it has been quite beneficial, but why does it alone now administer all affairs? **B.** Because it not only contains both human and divine sciences most abundantly, but it also expresses and explains them more successfully than all other languages. **A.** I will not set Greek or Hebrew against you—though I wish they were more common among us—but at least the modern vernacular languages <note>original: "vulgares saltem hodiernas" — the common spoken languages of the time like German, French, or English</note>, which serve all subjects and sciences no less successfully. **B.** If there is any such success in them, it is surely borrowed from Latin. **A.** It happens by our own fault; we have long since sworn allegiance to Latin, and we are so foolish that we do not work to either expand or polish our own mother tongues. **B.** As long as we use Latin conveniently, what need is there for another? **A.** Lest Latin should everywhere foist the most inept and irreligious men upon the Church, to whom the salvation of souls is entrusted for no other reason than that they can stammer in Latin. **B.** You are mistaken, for the Latin language presupposes a knowledge of the more humane arts <note>original: "humaniorum artium" — the "Humanities" or Liberal Arts, the traditional core of a gentleman's education</note>. **A.** You are mad to try to persuade us of that, when we daily endure the crudest ignorance of all things in those very men. **B.** So, will you henceforth hire laborers <note>original: "opifices" — common craftsmen or manual workers</note> and place them in the pulpits? **A.** What sarcasm! We are expected to adore whoever you eventually turn out from the Schools <note>original: "e Schola"</note>, even those who [cannot] even [speak] Latin...

### 16. ACONTIVS.
<note>This section refers to Jacobus Acontius (c. 1500–1566), a jurist and theologian known for his early advocacy of religious toleration.</note>

**A.** What reason should I say there is that, while in other matters men are most distrustful, they entrust their religion to Doctors <note>term: "Doctors" — here meaning highly educated theologians or university professors</note> with the utmost security? **B.** Because there is such constant assertion from the Prelates <note>original: "Antistitum"—high-ranking religious leaders or overseers</note> of our religion, and such valid refutation of the opposing side, that everyone considers it a sin not to believe men of such gravity and composed expression—men who are no doubt equally concerned about their own salvation, and most fair in examining the foundations of the opposing side. **A.** Meanwhile, that which should have been examined by many—indeed by nearly everyone—is committed to one, or at most a few. **B.** Deservedly so; for not everyone possesses such firm judgment that they may safely occupy themselves with the books of their adversaries. **A.** Yet would you wish the books of your own religion to be available to everyone and everywhere? **B.** One cannot hope for that, so great is the hatred of the truth. **A.** [And you wish] all the others to be extinguished? **B.** At least to be barred from the bookshops <note>original: "officinis"—shops or printers' workshops</note>. **A.** And yet, you condemn them by another's judgment, though they have been neither read, nor seen, nor corrected [by you]. **B.** I have no leisure to read that which I am already certain about. **A.** Nor do they have the leisure to read yours.

# APOTHEOSIS
<note>The term "apotheosis" refers to the process of a human being being elevated to the status of a god. Here, the author uses it sarcastically to describe how wealthy people are treated like saints after death.</note>

**B.** Were those people more foolish, or more wicked, who were prepared to admit the living Alexander <note>Alexander the Great, who famously sought divine honors during his lifetime.</note> into the number of the Gods for a price?

**A.** It is believable that none of them actually believed in Gods, and they were merely mocking the unwise.

**B.** The same thought comes to my mind whenever I look at today's <term>apotheosis</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀποθέωσιν" — the elevation of a person to divine status.</note>.

**A.** An Antichristian one?

**B.** Certainly, but specifically *our* kind; for as many funeral sermons or eulogies for the dead as I inspect, I seem to be able to count just as many new Gods.

**A.** I, on the contrary, see so many learned meditations on death and examples of a most praised life.

**B.** For whoever leaves behind as much money as suffices for a funeral procession and the payment of a petty priest, they are all treated as mirrors of a proven and imitable life.

**A.** Surely, as far as I know, if there were any flaws, they are never concealed.

**B.** And yet, I have never heard them called gluttons, blasphemers, adulterers, usurers, or jesters—or at least men conscious of their own weakness.

**A.** And they are presented as penitents?

**B.** Perhaps for one hour before death, at which time there is such a noisy rush to the Body of the Lord <note>The Eucharist or last rites.</note>, to prayer books, to alms-giving, to reconciliation, and to necessary patience, that you would think heaven was being stormed by force—all while that deaf man gradually stiffens into a Deity.

**A.** Even these people have a funeral memory.

**B.** A cold one indeed, and one that draws tears from no one. It is enough merely not to completely despair of their salvation, while those others, with great wailing... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "latu," likely "latratu" (wailing/barking) or "lamentatu" (lamentation).</note>

# THE WEALTHY.

...it would have been fitting for the practice of virtues, had they not been utterly depraved.

**A.** I would grant that, provided the poor were also pious in my eyes, even if they must go hungry.

**B.** You are mistaken; for it is not a lack of things, but humility of heart and "Christian poverty" that makes people good. If these traits exist in the midst of wealth, a person is innocent; but if they are absent even in the midst of hunger, you should expect no moderation.

**A.** I hear that they <note>the poor</note> get drunk, indulge in lust, and deceive the simple with strange frauds, commit robbery, and finally, even practice sorcery.

**B.** I have no answer to give, except that which was said to that famous pirate who plundered with a single small boat and was thus infamous, while Alexander the Great infested the whole world with an entire fleet. <note>This is a reference to a story from St. Augustine’s *City of God*, where a captured pirate tells Alexander that they are doing the same thing, but the pirate is called a thief because he has a small boat, while Alexander is called an emperor because he has a navy.</note>

**A.** Do those poor people shamefully squander the alms they receive?

**B.** These rich men swallow the blood of the poor in great bowls.

**A.** They <note>the poor</note> abuse the readiness of the pious.

**B.** In what way?

**A.** Through the generous hospitality of Guest-houses <term>xenodochia: institutions for housing pilgrims and strangers</term> and Hospitals <term>nosodochia: houses specifically for the sick</term>.

**B.** <note>The speaker is likely B here, responding to A’s defense of the rich</note> Bah! Look at the horse stables, the ball-courts <term>spheristeria: courts for playing ball games</term>, the gluttony of the orchestras, the feasts of the grooms, and the delights of the scoundrels. A single banquet of a rich man would be enough for the fullness and joy of a hundred beggars.

**A.** They [the poor] also have something to eat.

**B.** A single outfit of a rich man would satisfy the clothing needs of a hundred beggars.

**A.** They have something to cover themselves.

**B.** The decorations <note>original: "illinimenta" — literally "smears" or "coatings," referring to expensive wall-paintings, plasters, or gilding</note> of a single rich man's house could build small huts for a hundred poor people.

**A.** You are setting up illiterate rich men as your targets.

**B.** Those who seem to possess all learning are not a bit milder; for it is enough for them, like the Athenians, to know what is honorable, but to leave the doing of it to the Spartans <note>original: "Lacedaemoniis" — refers to a famous anecdote where the Athenians knew the right thing to do but did nothing, while the Spartans (Lacedaemonians) were the ones who actually acted on it.</note>.

**A.** I would hardly believe that Christ hides beneath the rags of a scoundrel, no matter how much he begs.

**B.** Nor do I; but I also believe the rich of our age are unworthy of Christ ever approaching them again in any guise of a poor man.

# 19. HYPOCRITES.

**A.** Up until now I have indeed erred, since I believed philosophers were wise, and physicians were health-giving, and legal experts were just, and theologians were religious; but now, what do you want me to do further? 

**B.** To know for certain that the whole world acts a play. <note>original: "universum mundum agere histrioniam." This is a reference to the "Theatrum Mundi" or "World as a Stage" trope, famously echoed later by Shakespeare.</note>

**A.** It appears so, for while all people present one thing outwardly, they seek another in reality. 

**B.** But you, avoid as carefully as possible those who possess more hypocrisy than others. 

**A.** Are there signs by which I may judge them? 

**B.** Hardly enough, but let these be your general ones: a wrinkled brow <note>to simulate deep thought or concern</note>, a composed gait, long robes, affected speech, and frequent pursuit of others' vices. 

**A.** Are those things evil, or merely suspicious? 

**B.** Put them to the test; you will find them to be slanderous, clingy, spiteful, and indeed bloodthirsty. 

**A.** But surely it should be easy, once they are betrayed by a single example, to strip them of the cloak of hypocrisy. 

**B.** You are mistaken; it is multifaceted and inexplicable due to its many entanglements. 

**A.** I don't know what is coming into my mind. 

**B.** What then? 

**A.** That those whom I always considered the best are actually hypocrites. 

**B.** That is not at all absurd, for in religion they are the most devoted, in the administration of law the most rigid, in the care of health the most superstitious, in the teaching of arts the most arrogant <note>original: "superciliosissimi," literally "having the most raised eyebrows"</note>, and in the rest of their lives they are the most orderly when in public; finally, they are the most generous in the distribution of titles. 

**A.** Must no one be trusted then? I believed these men were little saints. 

**B.** But you did not know that among them there are rivalries, <term>suggillationes: insults or slanders (literally "bruises")</term>, harrassments, then also <term>ignes fatuos: foolish fires or delusions</term>, vomitings, usury, and other things of that kind, as in the houses of the publicans...

### 20. SATIRISTS.

**A.** There has never been an age that did not have men to rebuke others. **B.** But those very men were hardly any better than the rest. **A.** Surely it is for the foolish to be able to note the vices of men and sting them with Satire. <note>original: "Satyra perstringere."</note> **B.** Quite easily; for such is the benefit of letters that, as if in a marketplace of masks, <note>original: "larvarum emporio." "Larva" refers to both theater masks and ghostly specters; the image suggests a world where people can buy and wear any personality they choose.</note> one may take on any face one pleases. **A.** It is the mark of an imprudent man to be unable to distinguish between the play of wit and serious matters. **B.** But those who play so much with the vigor of rhetoric, or mock us, might with that same ease recommend Satan to us. **A.** You are boiling over, my friend; for we were speaking of Satirists, yet you have flared up at the rashness of rhetoricians. **B.** I have composed myself: what do you wish to say in their praise? **A.** Doubtless... <note>original catchword: "Nimirum."</note>

<header>SATIRISTS.</header>

For even a harlot speaks excellently of chastity, a drunkard of sobriety, and a peddler of generosity. **A.** So it is with a poet regarding the most approved morals? **B.** I do not know whether to accuse them or the study of literature, which teaches us to be able to do all things. **A.** Consider the praises <term>encomia: formal speeches or pieces of writing that praise someone or something</term> of Nero, of Folly, of Baldness, of Gout, of Deafness, even of the Louse—did these perhaps offend you? <note>A refers to "paradoxical encomia," a popular Renaissance literary genre where authors wrote mock-praises of bad or trivial things, such as Erasmus's *Praise of Folly*.</note> **B.** Oh, if only the book markets <note>original: "Nundinae." Literally "fairs," referring to the major book fairs like those in Frankfurt or Leipzig where new works were sold.</note> did not bring us things worse than those! The traditional license granted to satirists to speak the truth through humor.</note> will always be harmless to good men. **A.** Freedom, certainly, but not insolence. **B.** Bah! As I have come to know the impieties of men of letters, I wonder that a vituperation of the most innocent Christ has not yet been written.

<header>21. THE EDUCATION OF A PRINCE.</header>

**A.** I will not wonder hereafter that the rule over so many men is entrusted to a single man, since all the arts and the benefits of nature are conferred upon that one person. **B.** Do you really believe that the sons of Heroes <note>original: "Heroum"; here referring to the children of great leaders or royal bloodlines</note> are shaped more precisely, and are more fortunate than those of the common lot? **A.** Indeed, they are formed both more efficiently and more faithfully. For those things which cost us great labor, and must almost be wrested from the envious, lie open to them with every ease and readiness. **B.** Is this why they are wise and brave beyond the human condition, and act as saviors to the world? **A.** So I believe. **B.** And yet, many of them frankly admit their own weaknesses, and then cast the burdens of government <note>original: "regiminis"</note> upon others. **A.** That is only fitting; for who, unless he were hundred-eyed and hundred-handed, <term>centoculus & centimanus: references to Argus Panoptes and the Hekatonkheires of Greek myth, symbols of total vigilance and immense power to work</term> could be sufficient for all things? **B.** I do not mean that, but rather that those who are unworthy and equipped with nothing sometimes hold the rudders <note>original: "clavos"; literally the tillers or steering oars of a ship, a common metaphor for steering the state</note> of empire themselves, so that the craft of ruling is a matter of violence rather than diligence. **A.** You suspect that to be the case. **B.** I am certain of it; for I could produce for you from the histories barbers, and harp-players, and gamblers, and gluttons—and, what might surprise you, pimps and charlatans <term>circulatores: itinerant peddlers or performers, often used as a derogatory term for swindlers</term>—who have commanded kings. **A.** How well you think the Kingdoms have been provided for! <note>A's comment here is likely sarcastic, noting the absurdity of such low-born advisors.</note> **B.** Perhaps neither more happily nor worse; for I believe the very mass of the empire and such a great number of men preserves itself. **A.** Does not everything glorious done anywhere yield to the glory of the Prince? **B.** Truly; for they hold the praise for buildings, for counsels, for statutes, for confessions <note>original: "confessionum"; likely referring to formal declarations of faith or legal decrees</note>, and for victories.

### 23. THE HUNGRY.

<margin>A.</margin> I remember it being occasionally thrown against Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the Stoic philosopher and advisor to Nero, who was often criticized for his vast personal wealth while writing in praise of the simple life</note> that he frequently praised poverty while, in the meantime, possessing almost royal treasures. **B.** I think the learned are being attacked through Seneca’s side <note>meaning that Seneca is being used as a proxy to mock all intellectuals who preach what they do not practice</note>. **A.** To me, scholars truly seem to be the most in need of all mortals. **B.** Not those who know how to fish with letters as if with hooks. ## 24. *THE GOOD.*

**A.** The world is full of fools. <note>original: "Stultorum plena sunt omnia"; a common Latin proverb often attributed to Cicero</note> **B.** That is a haughty thing to say; you smell of a pretentious philosopher. **A.** Will you deny it? **B.** I will speak more moderately, alongside **Plato**, saying that men who are exceedingly good or exceedingly bad are very few, but those in the middle are the most numerous. **A.** <margin>^</margin> Why is it then that the people rush into every foolish thing and establish it with such widespread agreement? **B.** That happens because of the talkative wickedness of teachers or rulers, who so greatly abuse the simple credulity and readiness of the people. **A.** You are mistaken; for if they could be led anywhere, they would certainly be brought more often to virtues and piety whenever they obtain good teachers. **B.** You cannot be ignorant of what can be obtained from the people if you look even briefly at the luxury of courts, the ornaments of temples, the leisure of **Academies**, the labors of military camps, the rules of religious orders, and the frequency of extortions and "shearings." <note>original: "detonsionum"; literally "shearings," a metaphor for the heavy taxation or financial exploitation of the populace, as if they were sheep</note> Moreover, the people are not so insane that they do not understand better things if they are shown, or if they are substituted for worse ones. **A.** What if perhaps you do not know with what labors or prayers these things were obtained from the common people? **B.** By what others, if not by painted eloquence <note>original: "fucata eloquentia"; deceptive or "made-up" rhetoric</note> and simulated holiness—and finally, by disguised force or a hypocritical tyranny? Believe me, it is a very light thing to beg for the wealth, sweat, and blood of the common folk if there is an honorable pretext—such is the integrity of men even now. **A.** You seem to me to be truly ignorant of the hardness and harshness of men—

### 25. THE ACADEMIES.

**A.** However many have ever soared into the breeze of a good reputation, they seem to me to have been raised up on the wings of **Logic** <term>Dialectices: The formal art of logical argument and reasoning</term> and **Rhetoric** <term>Rhetorices: The art of persuasive speaking and writing</term>. **B.** You have named two plagues of the human race. **A.** You mock the names, but I understand them as the arts of discovering and persuading the truth. **B.** Plausible enough, but I don't want them even then. **A.** Are you hostile to the truth? **B.** Not at all, but to the **"Lesbian rule."** <note>original: "Lesbiæ regulæ"; a classical metaphor for a flexible mason's rule that bends to the shape of the stone, used here to describe a standard of truth that is shifted to suit the speaker's needs</note> **A.** Explain yourself. **B.** Naturally, that is suspect to me

For just as in a public square most things are for sale for luxury and excess, yet some things are also for practical use and for piety, so the Academies—however hostile to Christ and for the most part opposed to him in every way—still possess books and men who are supporters of Christian truth. **A.** Where then should I learn that which Christ requires? **B.** Wherever you wish, so long as it is more successfully than in such schools. **A.** But will you have to show me which school you actually approve of?

### 26. AN AWAKENING.

**A.** Whenever those good men come to mind who were suffocated under the tyranny of the Papacy <term>Papatus: the office or jurisdiction of the Pope; here used critically in a Reformation context</term> together with the emerging truth, I grow entirely angry with the World, which is plainly incurable. **B.** And yet, in the previous age, almost the entire world woke up and returned to the light of religion, the arts, and governance. **A.** To be sure, it had to be loudly called out, rebuked, and convicted. **B.** I do not believe the matter was conducted with greater effort than in the past, but rather that it was reserved for the maturity of our own time. **A.** But truth is always the same, as is its reason and evidence; nor do I believe those men were so very different from us. Why then did they not achieve the same against the Roman yoke as our own people have? **B.** First, you will consider that a new [understanding] of liberty or truth... <note>original: "veritatis"</note>

...[of] truth, but for a long time it creeps into the minds of men, and flies about in silent whispers and complaints; finally, it begins to threaten I know not what with somewhat bolder words. <note>original: "ritatis curā" — likely completing "veritatis curā" (out of a care for truth) from the previous page.</note> **A.** Go on, I like this. **B.** Know this: unless some violent injury or evident necessity approaches, or the hope of a happier and easier attempt shines forth, all the best things sink down again due to human sluggishness and softness. **A.** Well said. **B.** But if some noble and talented mind arises, a wonderful hope provokes even the silent ones, and easily leads those who are ready into an open profession of their beliefs. **A.** That is plausible. **B.** And so, what was for a long time the secret wish of many is believed to be the persuasion of a single man. **A.** I agree. **B.** Afterward, when the faction grows into greater strength <term>nervos: literally "sinews" or "nerves," referring here to the power and organizational force of a movement</term>, it acts more confidently for its own sake and attacks what belongs to others; and generally, it overturns the first moderate counsels and the most prudent original plan. **A.** Bravo! **B.** Finally, it grows into such a mass that it becomes both a burden and a source of fear to its own author. **A.** It is apparent. **B.** Now you yourself shall judge why, at the first voice of **Luther**, the **Germans** rose up so eagerly and in such numbers—namely, weary of the **Roman yoke** <note>The "Roman yoke" refers to the perceived political and financial oppression of the German states by the Papacy in Rome.</note> and its perfidy rather than its obscured Religion, and thereafter they were full of threats against the **Pope**. But not even they themselves were thinking of such a great desertion, until, spurred by greater injuries, they first loosened the chains from their tongues and pens, and soon after from their hands. Finally, as the hatred of **Rome** grew into various factions, new wounds were made in the **Church**, and new lamentations were caused, which I fear no one except **Christ** can heal. **A.** Let us pray to **Christ**, that He who has often given us **Heroes** through whom the **Christian** world could be said to be reborn, will not deny us perhaps the last physician for the **Church**.

### 27. PEDAGOGISM.
<note>original: "Paedagogismus" — This section crituques the "schoolmaster" mindset: an obsession with rules and rote learning over practical action.</note>

**A.** Why is it that masters of letters <note>original: "literarum magistri"</note>, when brought forward to handle public affairs, are the most inept of all **mortals**? **B.** Because they never direct their minds toward such worthless things, but cling to a more sublime speculation of human affairs. **A.** But if someone were to catch them in that very citadel of speculation, he would find them sweating over sentence constructions, and anomalies, and irregular words <term>heteroclitis: nouns or verbs that deviate from standard patterns of declension or conjugation—the "irregularities" of grammar</term>. **B.** These are the doors of the arts, which it is just as right to open for the youth as it is to open the inner chambers of wisdom. **A.** But if someone should happen to enter, will he find them to be wise men, or merely pointers toward wisdom? **B.** Wise men, certainly; otherwise they would be showing off wisdom for a price, like a dancing bear on a chain. **A.** Or do you really get anything else from them besides: "thus **Cicero** thinks," "thus **Plato**," "thus **Aristotle**"; "this is the piety of **Regulus**," "this the integrity of **Brutus**," "this the chastity of **Lucretia**"? <note>Regulus, Brutus, and Lucretia were standard Roman historical examples used to teach moral virtues in schools.</note> **B.** Is it not enough to have guides and advisors for all the best things? **A.** But you were just calling them wise men, whom you now admit are mere guides or dictionaries. **B.** Yet how great an excellence it is to know so many things. **A.** It would be better to know the best things and to *do* them; instead, just as little birds carry seeds in their beaks to their chicks without being fed themselves <note>original: "faturatæ" — likely a variation of "saturatæ" (sated/filled)</note>, so these men pluck from all the books just so they might have...

<header>28. COMMENTARIES.</header>

<margin>*A.*</margin> At the very name of the **Apocalypse** <note>original: "Apocalypfeos" — the Book of Revelation, the final book of the New Testament known for its complex and terrifying imagery</note>, I once trembled with a certain religious awe, just as I have always done. <margin>*B.*</margin> Always those, indeed, who adapted their prophecies to appearances and specific people have attempted too much; but to have clung to general suspicions of changes—that, at last, is the safest path. <margin>*A.*</margin> That, however, is nothing compared to the **Prophetic Spirit** by which they wished to appear driven; for it is also the mark of a wise man to guess not inconveniently about the future <note>A suggests that "playing it safe" with vague guesses is merely human prudence, not the divine inspiration these commentators claim to possess</note>. <margin>*B.*</margin> I do not see what has lured good men into this rash attempt at prophesying. <margin>*A.*</margin> Nor do I, except that I suspect that "formula" by which they explain all the mysteries of the Prophets gave them hope and courage to touch even upon the prognostics of the times. <margin>*B.*</margin> What formula? <margin>*A.*</margin> The one by which—whatever the Prophet finally intended—they forge from every text either a spear for dispute <note>original: "difputatorium iaculum" — a rhetorical weapon used in theological arguments</note>, or they shape civil morals, or they demonstrate some clever trick of Rhetoric; the rest (unless something happens to fit Christ) they reserve for the **Heavenly Academy** <note>A sarcastic reference to the idea that difficult passages can only be understood in the afterlife</note>. <margin>*B.*</margin> What greater honesty is there than to explain those things which you know, and to leave the rest to God? <margin>*A.*</margin> The honesty is greater if you confess that you do not grasp divine mysteries at all, and rest content with what has been revealed. <margin>*B.*</margin> What use would there be for the Prophets without interpreters? <margin>*A.*</margin> What use is there for them *with* this sort of interpretation, which—whether it even touches the Prophet's meaning from afar—is uncertain? We shall pray...

# HERETICS.

G 5

*A:* ...Do you believe there are as many sects as those hateful names commonly bandied about?

*A:* <note>Speaker A is responding to his own rhetorical question or a missing prompt from the previous page.</note> Certainly, for an ambitious mind is hardly born that has not sought a following of error and a trail of disciples.

*B:* You do not agree with me.

*A:* But the multitude of sects is clearly visible.

*B:* Names, surely; but they seem to me to have been thought up more quickly to stir up hatred than claimed by the authors of any actual disagreement.

*A:* At last, you will play the patron to heretics!

*B:* Yes, especially since the reach of that name is so great that it can be cast upon even the most innocent person as easily as it is done by a great consensus.

*A:* Watch what you say; it is no light thing to excuse a heretic, and to defend one is even most dangerous.

*B:* Once, perhaps; now it is a matter of "theological liberality" <note>original: "Theologicae liberalitatis" — likely a sarcastic jab at the way scholars or inquisitors used the pretense of a "fair hearing" to trap their opponents.</note> to hear out a heretic.

*A:* I beg you, do not suspect such a thing of men so conscientious and circumspect, who fear nothing more than the wounds of the Church <note>original: "Ecclesiae vulnera"</note> or strive to avoid them.

*B:* I am not unaware of the error by which they usually sin; for since they suspect the very worst of those who are more free-thinking, they suborn their own lackeys <term>mancipia: literally "slaves," here referring to subordinates or agents used to do someone's dirty work</term> to ambush good and unsuspecting men. They do not merely accept the fabricated accusations <term>delationes: formal denunciations, often associated with informants</term> of these people, but they even publish them and attack them with a marvelous zeal.

*A:* No excuse from the innocent moves them here, no protestation.

*B:* None; but by God’s judgment it happens that a scoundrel—nay, even an adulteress or a poisoner making an accusation—is believed with great applause rather than a man of the highest character who asserts his innocence <note>original: "innocentiam"</note> before God.

*A:* I would appeal to the judgment of the entire world.

*B:* That judgment, of course, by which Christ <note>original: "Christus"</note> was condemned, and where whoever is most powerful and most talkative most easily wins his case.

# HERETICS.

*A.* Posterity will judge.

*B.* How can it, when they alone have the printers <term>Typographos: early modern printing house owners who held significant power over whose ideas were published</term> at their beck and call? It is by these resources that they are able to touch the heavens with their mouths and traverse the lands with their tongues. Meanwhile, whoever does not worship the statue <note>A reference to the biblical story of King Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 3, where those who refused to bow to his golden image were thrown into a furnace.</note> shall be burned.

*A.* From where does such a heat of hatred come?

*B.* From excessive self-love and self-admiration. For if we turned our hatred against ourselves—that is, against our own flesh and the rebellion of our spirit—we would easily grant some indulgence to a brother who errs or disagrees.

*A.* If they were more knowledgeable, you would wish them to be more merciful.

*B.* In all cases; for in this way those ill-fated names <note>original: "infausta illa nomina" — referring to sectarian labels like 'Lutheran,' 'Calvinist,' or 'Papist' used as insults.</note> would easily vanish—names which tear the Church apart and expose her to the rebukes of her enemies.

*A.* I certainly will restrain myself hereafter, and I beg forgiveness for the fault which the authority of men imposed upon me.

*B.* Do you not know that nothing is so foolish that it has not been said by some "wise" man? <note>original: "nihil tam stultum esse, quod non ab aliquo sapiente dictum sit" — a famous aphorism from Cicero's *De Divinatione*.</note>

### 33. RELIGION.

*A.* I have very conveniently been freed from a great danger today.

*B.* Is that so? I congratulate you.

*A.* I give thanks both to you and to him through whom I now believe more cautiously.

*B.* What kind of talk is this? Can one even believe "incautiously"?

*A.* Quite easily. For if I happen to believe a proposition that seems very sound and straightforward to me, there might be a tiny word hidden in it that gives birth to the most dangerous consequences. Thus it happens that, being unaware, I might believe impiously.

*B.* And so, are you then guilty of impiety?

*A.* Entirely. Hence it is that I am even now devising formulas in my mind for believing most cautiously hereafter.

*B.* I, who [look] to your heights...

# RELIGION.

I never climb to such heights; with a simple and almost rustic faith I grasp those things which I see are consistent with Scripture, nor am I so timid regarding specific words that I fear falling into an unconscious heresy from them. 

*A.* See how careless you are. Did Christ not suffer?

*B.* Yes indeed, to Him be the glory. 

*A.* Tell me then, according to what <term>kind of communication: referring to the *communicatio idiomatum*, the theological doctrine regarding how the divine and human natures of Christ share attributes</term> did He suffer?

*B.* That I certainly do not know. 

*A.* Oh, you unfortunate man! And was that passion a result of the <note>original: "voluntatis Divinæ antecedentis, an consequentis" — scholastic distinctions between God's "antecedent" will (His primary desire, such as the salvation of all) and "consequent" will (His will in light of human circumstances or the Fall).</note> antecedent Divine will, or the consequent? 

*B.* I know that God willed it. 

*A.* Oh, you wretch! In the order of causes, did God's counsel concerning the passion precede the creation, or did it follow it? 

*B.* I give thanks to my Redeemer, and I do not inquire further into His hidden counsel. 

*A.* You see, surely, that by paying so little attention you fall into a chaos of heresies, and you do not even believe according to the <term>commonplaces: the standard categories or organized topics of systematic theology</term> of our religion. 

*B.* I believe the creeds and the summary of our religion which Holy Scripture offers me of its own accord: the magnitude of my own misery, the vastness of Divine mercy, the struggle of the Christian warfare, and the practice of prescribed piety. 

*A.* It is not enough to know these generalities; one must also mark the <note>original: "scopuli" — literally "rocks" or "reefs." A common metaphor for theological pitfalls or errors that lead to spiritual shipwreck.</note> rocks upon which human curiosity has struck, lest the same happen to you on the path of salvation. 

*B.* Indeed, just as new laws create new crimes, so do these new "commonplaces" create new heretics. 

*A.* Do not joke in a serious matter. 

*B.* I will confess to you that I once rashly attempted such a thing, but when that investigation into those "rocks" repeatedly supplied new troubles to my mind, I first wished that all memory of them were cast out of my soul; then, with all the strength I could, I blocked all my senses and composed myself to a humble obedience to Christ. Since then I have become more tranquil, nor does anything disturb me except the memory of my former curiosity...

### 34. DEATH.

*B.* The poor man rests in the lap of his mother <note>referring to "Mother Earth," the common grave of all.</note>.
*A.* The rich man buys heaven.
*B.* The poor man sells it, yet does not lack it. <note>original: "pauper vendit, nec caret" — likely an allusion to the Gospel passage where one sells all they have to gain the kingdom, or perhaps suggesting the poor man "gives" the kingdom to others through his example.</note>
*A.* The rich man departs from this life amid the embraces of his friends.
*B.* The poor man flies upward among the company of angels.

But what need is there for this troublesome back-and-forth? Truly, it is never more clearly revealed how faithless riches are, and how faithful poverty is, than at the moment of a person’s death. For this is that exact point at which we implore in vain all those protections upon which we have leaned until now: that sky—supposedly so observant of our needs—the favorable stars, the earth as our servant, the sciences as the wings of our loftiness, wealth as the instrument of our will, and friends as the retinue of our desires. We find Religion to have been a mere lid to cover our wickedness, <note>original: "Religionem nequitiæ operculum"</note> fame to be a most foul flatterer, and Philosophy to be a strength made of paper. <note>original: "Philosophiam robur papiraceum" — a vivid metaphor for academic arguments that provide no real support in the face of mortality.</note> Finally, we see all of nature—which we thought was uniquely intent upon us (if God so pleased!), proud of our favor, and impatient at the thought of our departure—to be indifferent. Who would not laugh at how we are then mocked? For we seem to ourselves to die as a great evil to the world and an inestimable loss to the earth, laden as we are with so many gifts and endowments which the best...

# MARTYRIUM.
## 67

...hinge of religion stood, they have at least relied upon the dreams of certain imposters. This makes me suspect that it is easier to lead the innocent common folk to the slaughterhouse <note>original: "lanienam." Literally a butcher's stall or shambles; here referring to the site of execution or martyrdom.</note> than to persuade the more prudent <note>original: "cordatioribus." *A.* What you have said is indeed deplorable; yet since after the Apostles—the first heralds of our faith—the most learned men, those most skilled in all **Philosophy**, and even those powerful in world affairs, did not hesitate to testify to this "ridiculous and absurd sect of Christians" (as people say) through a wretched death and punishment, and seemed to demonstrate something unusual and beyond the strength of nature, who could doubt that this is the summit of human confession, which is made through blood?

*B.* I would believe that for converting and moving the multitude, nothing is more effective than martyrdom, which strikes the eyes and seems to presuppose everything. However, for those concerned with the highest certainty of religion, it is not sufficient.

*A.* Believe me, whenever I come across the **Martyrology** <note>original: "Martyrologium." *B.* It is a pity that reading it is less frequent among our students.

*A.* Evidently, everyone considers themselves to have that solid and unshakable religion which would suffice for martyrdom.

*B.* May God see to that, for it belongs to Him alone to animate us for such an arduous trial. Otherwise, as I know the constancy of men and their concern for religion, I believe most would defend their opinions only up to—but not including—the fire <note>original: "usque ad ignem exclusive." A cynical idiom suggesting people are brave in their beliefs until the moment they are actually threatened with being burned at the stake.</note>.

# 38. PRAYERS.
## 68

*A.* Among so many little books of prayer, both old and recent alike, which one would you recommend to me as a familiar companion?

*B.* Why do you ask? The one which necessity—the most eloquent and ingenious of all things—has created.

*A.* Who is that author? Or what trifles are you playing at?

*B.* I speak seriously; I believe no formula is more perfect than that which the **Cross of Christ** <note>original: "Crux Christi." Referring here to the experience of suffering and sacrifice as the truest teacher of how to pray.</note> has dictated.

*A.* Would you call those sobs, gasps, and disordered cries "prayers"?

*B.* Do you really think the charms of words and a structure of speech recited from a sheet of paper can persuade God of anything?

*B.* Is the **Lord’s Prayer** <term>dominica oratio: The "Our Father," the central prayer of Christianity taught by Jesus to his disciples.</term> not sufficient for you, to which not even the entire world could add or subtract anything? *A.* You do not yet understand me. There are various failings of human weakness, various types of temptations and afflictions, and various walks of life. *B.* Perhaps; though a devotion must be very cold indeed if it must seek fire from little books—not to mention that God understands the mute just as well.

## 71

...[so that] you would believe them born for the comforts and aids of the human race.

**A.** I praise your simplicity; for this makes you bear your yoke more gently, and it sustains you most clearly through the admiration of the most worthless things. **B.** In your opinion, then, shall we entrust religion to the stupid, erudition to fools, morals to barbarians, and empires to slaves?

**A.** These are the words of literary pride. For me, however, it is most sweet to have learned through long experience and intimate conversation that those men are not better or more certain of things than others, but only more slippery and talkative.

## 40.- CONVERSATION.

**A.** How unfair is my lot, never to have been admitted among the weightier colloquies and the most prudent consultations of those on whom the entire state and the Republic of Letters <term>Republic of Letters: The "Respublica Literaria," the international community of scholars and intellectuals who shared ideas via correspondence during the 17th and 18th centuries.</term> depend.

**B.** Why do you strike such a tragic tone here?

**A.** What else [should I feel], but the surges of thoughts from those men who—having never been examined by the censures of the most Excellent men, nor ever composed or subdued—riot among themselves under the shadows of poverty and obscurity? Meanwhile, you most fortunate ones possess the domestic decisions of all things with a great shortcut, and even now you either bring up the newborn offspring of your genius <note>A common metaphor for a scholar's books or intellectual theories.</note> to the most exacting judgments of your approved [critics]...

## 41. THE BANQUET

**A.** Have you heard anything about our banquet yesterday? **B.** That "philosophical" one, which eventually ended like a feast of the Cyclopes? <note>original: "cyclopicum." ...most perfect in languages, Zwinger <note>Theodor Zwinger the Elder (1533–1588), a Swiss physician and scholar famous for his massive encyclopedia, the *Theatrum Humanae Vitae* (Theater of Human Life).</note>, that noble actor of the human scene; Gessner <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565), a Swiss polymath whose "Universal Bibliography" was a monumental effort to catalog all known books to prevent their loss.</note>, the admirable antagonist of oblivion; besides many others—whom do they have today who would dare compare himself to them? **A.** I do not know what to say, for you have terrified me with such great names; I struggle greatly even to seek out and present the "lights" of our own age to oppose them. **B.** This is what I must further guard you against: do not be too generous with the titles of "erudition" and "knowledge." Do not trade in every superficial veneer <note>original: "fuco." Otherwise, you will bring forth men who are doubtful, groomed, and merely gilded—not solid, precious, and truly golden. You may find many who are similar in their titles and outward form, but very few who are equal to the ancients in weight and true value. This is no insult to those who—ignoring the judgment of the common crowd—follow their ancestors in serious and successful emulation.

**A.** I feel quite dejected; <note>original: "Male mihi est." Literally "it is bad for me," expressing a sense of being corrected or humbled.</note> I who until now have accepted as truly learned those who only held the name of the learned, and I am wounded.

### THE MASTER.

...he will use the primary **language of Europe** <note>original: "lingua Europæ primaria." Likely referring to Latin as the universal scholarly tongue.</note>, whether in bound verse or in free prose, with the greatest readiness. Then, he will untie all things called into doubt and distribute them with an exquisite method most ingeniously. Soon, with a river of words and the little flowers of elegance, he will draw the ears of his listeners wherever he wishes; thereafter, he will gaze into the mysteries of numbers and the infinite charms of proportions, and accommodate them to human affairs. He will also make melody with sound and the harmony of voices, both for himself and for others. 

But if something must be measured, no shape—if something must be weighed, no mass—will escape the sagacity and strength of his intellect. No star will rotate in the heavens without his knowledge, nor will anything threaten the earth without his awareness. For he, being aware of all the secrets of **Nature**, foretells what the air portends, what the earth brings forth, how the sea seethes, what the mountains "cook" <note>original: "coquant." In early modern science, it was believed minerals and metals "ripened" or "cooked" inside mountains.</note>, how animals interact, and what man—the **microcosm** <note>original: "microcosmus." The philosophical idea that man is a "little world" reflecting the structure of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note>—comprehends in himself; he accurately investigates and most skillfully explains what the command of our soul is and what the governance of the body is. 

Finally, he is led to rule men, whose minds he first tames, then softens their habits, and finally, through the contemplation of the future life, renders them initiated into **divinity**.

**A.** Oh, what a distinguished man! One truly to be honored—not merely with a doctoral cap, a ring, and the useless light of torches or the noise of trumpets <note>original: "taratantarae strepitu." *Taratantara* is an onomatopoeic word for the sound of a trumpet.</note>—but to be lifted up plainly upon our shoulders. But I see such a man nowhere. 

**B.** That happens because of the dullness of wits, which do not grasp so many and such great things. 

**A.** Meanwhile, every year a swarm <note>original: "examen." Literally a "swarm" (as of bees), here used to describe a graduating class or crowd of students.</note> of these men comes forth to us, who—oh, if only...

## 46. H E R O E S.

*A.* O hail, **Heroes**, as many of you as have deserved the very best from the human race. *B.* What is this devotion of yours? *A.* Here indeed I walk about in the **Hall of Heroes**, and I contemplate with admiration and reverence the faces of those who excelled among men. *B.* What indeed comes to mind when you look upon these **images of virtue** <note>original: "virtutum iconas." The speaker is likely looking at a gallery of portraits or statues representing historical or mythological heroes.</note>? *A.* I take note of whether **Nature** has fabricated a structure of any rarer quality <note>original: "rarioris Naturæ ædificii." Referring to the physical bodies or countenances of the heroes as "buildings" for their souls.</note> in which she might worthily house such noble souls. *B.* To me, however, there first occur those monsters with which they were forced to fight with such labor and diligence, and then the unworthy gratitude of the World, which they obtained despite so many merits. *A.* Indeed, what greater reward for labors can there be than that they stand forth in the **Temple of Memory** and good fame for all posterity, and challenge all the more noble minds—

# HEROES.

...call them, and having been received as if into the number of the **Gods** <note>original: "Deorum." In this context, it refers to "excellence" or "manly worth" rather than just moral piety.</note>. But because they pitied human errors discovered everywhere, they sought out remedies with great effort; yet when these remedies ought to have been applied and received with great applause, they were shamefully hissed away. This is why I call those men wretched, who, after long exhaustion and provoked by the incurability of human nature, cursed both their own labors and the earth itself, departing from this life in indignation. *A.* Then, in your judgment, no one should be occupied with reforming human affairs? *B.* On the contrary, all the best men will be—but under the certain expectation of infamy, exhaustion, and ingratitude. This is what all reformers of governments, **sciences**, and **religions** have experienced. *A.* Let it suffice that they at least satisfied their own standards. *B.* Even that is not allowed; so great is the diversity of opinions, or rather the force of the Divine Decree, which commands the **World** <note>original: "Mundum."</note> to be entirely unfaithful to us. *A.* Something must be tried. *B.* Go then, and like the most noble **Brahe** <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the famous Danish astronomer. Despite his groundbreaking work, he was eventually forced to leave his observatory on the island of Hven due to political disagreements.</note>, drive those monstrous spheres and **eccentric epicycles** <term>eccentrepiciclos: complex geometric circles used in early astronomy to explain why planets appeared to move at different speeds and directions.</term> from the heavens with great expense and most ingenious instruments, while you yourself are driven out from your own lands by barbarian force.

### 49. *FABLES.*

*A.* I am often accustomed to being angry with historians, who have dared to sell the most fabulous <note>original: "fabulosissimas." In this context, it refers to stories that are legendary, fictitious, or mythical rather than factual.</note> things as truths, as if posterity would possess no judgment of its own. *B.* However great their fault often is, I do not doubt that many things are now believed by us to be fables which were once most true. For if anyone should look a little more closely at the darkness of certain times, the impieties of some, and the cruelties of others, and compare them with more fortunate ages, he can never be amazed enough. *A.* But who would ever believe that the reason of almost the entire human race could wander so far that, with truth discovered nowhere, it is occupied by the most foolish opinions and rests under the most shameful empire of errors? *B.* Look at least, then, at the height of the Antichrist, upon what follies and absurdities it was founded; nevertheless, it grew into an admirable mass and almost invincible power, so that not even now, though brought forth in the clear light, does it cease to do harm and to persuade. *A.* How great the force of religion is, even Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing Roman religious rites to civilize the early populace.</note>, and Muhammad, and then Serisius <note>Likely a reference to a specific historical or contemporary figure used as an example of a religious leader or deceiver.</note> have taught me. Meanwhile, no one shall persuade me that there was no one in those centuries who opposed himself to such great impostors, and who [uncovered] such fabulous schemes...

A deformed and shapeless shape! **A.** Do you not know that sacrifices must now be made to these idols, to these gods?

# 52. COURTLY MATHEMATICS.

**A.** Who can show me a Mathematician? 
**B.** Do you not know that this race of men is condemned by the laws? <note>original: "legibus damnatum." Under Roman law, particularly the Code of Justinian, "mathematicians" were often legally equated with forbidden astrologers and sorcerers.</note> 
**A.** I am not looking to inquire into another’s life; I am looking out for my own, at least. 
**B.** But it is not even fitting to be curious about one’s own life. 
**A.** I do not want a fortune-teller, but a master of the finest arts. 
**B.** Of which ones, then? 
**A.** First, of Arithmetic. 
**B.** Stifel <note>Michael Stifel (1487–1567), a famous German monk and mathematician who wrote "Arithmetica Integra."</note> will teach that exactly, or our own Henisch <note>Georg Henisch (1549–1618), a physician and mathematician from Augsburg.</note>. 
**A.** I do not want that kind; I want one who can calculate <note>original: "subducam." A pun on "subducere," which means both to calculate a sum and to stealthily withdraw or divert something.</note> well how much is needed to win my master’s favor. Then, I need a Geometer. 
**B.** Not the Euclid of Clavius? <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612) was a Jesuit astronomer and mathematician who produced a famous commentary on Euclid.</note> 
**A.** No, but one who can teach the exact proportion between a **crooked** Master and a **straight** servant. <note>A satirical play on the geometric definitions of "curved" and "rectilinear" lines vs. moral "crookedness" and "rectitude."</note> Afterward, a Musician. 
**B.** Will Aristoxenus or Lassus <note>Aristoxenus was an ancient Greek music theorist; Orlande de Lassus (1532–1594) was one of the most famous composers of the late Renaissance.</note> do nothing for you here? 
**A.** Clearly nothing, for the master’s monochord <term>monochord: an ancient musical instrument with a single string used to measure mathematical intervals; here it refers to the master's temperament or mood</term> must be "dissected" in a different way. But I would also like an Astronomer. 
**B.** What do you think of Ptolemy or Copernicus? 
**A.** They do not satisfy me, for they do not properly define for me the rising and setting of the "luminaries." <note>A satirical reference to the "rising and falling stars" of the court—prominent officials and favorites.</note> But where will an Astrologer be found? 
**B.** Let Cardan <note>Gerolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a brilliant polymath and astrologer.</note> alone be more than enough. 
**A.** But he never taught me how to observe the true motions of **wandering** Councilors. <note>original: "errantium Consiliariorum." A pun on "errantia sidera," the wandering stars (planets), and erratic or misguided court advisors.</note> Next, I also have need of an Optician. 
**B.** Let Maurolico help, or Marolois. <note>Francesco Maurolico and Samuel Marolois were renowned 16th-century writers on optics and perspective.</note> 
**A.** They do not know how the rays of the master’s favor are refracted toward me; they do not know the "point of the foot." <note>original: "pede punctum." In optics, the "foot of the perpendicular" or "pedal point"; here it likely refers to knowing exactly where one stands with a superior.</note> I have even less hope for a master of Catoptrics <term>catoptrics: the branch of optics dealing with mirrors and reflections</term>. 
**B.** Johannes Pena <note>original: "Iohannes Persan." Likely referring to Jean Pena (1528–1558), a French mathematician who edited works on Euclid and optics.</note> is recommended. 
**A.** Only if he had designed a mirror that would reveal my master’s secret passions and his various dispositions.

### § 3. CHRISTIAN 
### MATHEMATICS.

**B.** Can you now also bear my Mathematics? 
**A.** I can indeed, unless you laugh at my misfortunes. 
**B.** Truly, my art is not ridiculous to me, but yours—or the one you seek—seems wretched. 
**A.** Reveal it then, if you have anything serious and solid. 
**B.** First, then, remember that in my **Arithmetic**, the **Trinity** <note>original: "Trinarium"</note> is sacred to me and to be adored; by its power, everything else exists, is numbered, and is preserved. Next, one must admire the proportion of the Divine circle to the human line, from which every measurement of created things flows. Third, the weight of the most innocent blood <note>A reference to the sacrifice of Christ.</note> is so great that it lifts the entire earthly globe, and its power is such that it separates the good from the evil. Fourth, there is that harmony <note>original: "concentum"</note> of divine and human things, which the human mind cannot grasp and no music can foreshadow. From these things my **Astronomy** arises, which teaches the origins, progressions, and phenomena of the Church; it fixes Christ as the Sun in the center, then marks the stars—that is, the lights of the saints—and carries us away into imitation and wonder by the movement of the heavenly choir. **Optics** also refracts the divine gifts within us, and the most clear mirror of the life of Christ is the summit of our perspective. **Geodesy** <note>term: "Geodesy" (Gæodeſia); the science of measuring and monitoring the Earth's size and shape.</note> is easy, if we at least learn to measure ourselves and our earthly beds; and **Cosmography** to anyone...

->MATH. CHRIST.<-

**A.** Always in a ship? 

**B.** Nay, even an Island, which the sea of the World attacks on all sides but never moves, let alone displaces; for from the word of God we have a most fortified castle <note>original: "castrum"</note>, which those who have brought forth words, or reason, or dreams, or deceptions, or threats against Him—by whose nod this entire universe subsists in nothingness—have besieged in vain until now.

# § 4. THE TRIUMPH OF VANITY.

*A.* Is it permitted to even recount dreams? *B.* One may recount them, but it is proper to despise <note>original: "despuere"; literally "to spit upon" or reject with contempt.</note> them. *A.* Yet it is pleasant to be happy even while sleeping. *B.* Do you not know how often gold is accustomed to turn into dung? <note>A common proverbial warning that the "gold" found in dreams usually turns out to be worthless waste upon waking.</note> *A.* Listen anyway, then judge as you see fit. *B.* Recount it, dreamer. *A.* In that time, when we were dancing everywhere with insolent joy, I saw Vanity triumphing. *B.* What is the wonder, since we see that daily and with groaning. *A.* But this vision of mine was consistent in all its parts. *B.* You seem to have seen something entirely vainer than vanity itself; tell it then. *A.* First, Talkativeness stepped forward with a trumpet, I suppose in the place of Fame, to summon spectators; Painting and the Printing Press <note>original: "prælum"; the inclusion of the printing press here suggests that Vanity is spread through published works and visual arts.</note> served her as handmaids. *B.* A sufficiently worthy beginning. *A.* Then, with great weariness, followed two most scrawny little horses, called Labor and Fidelity. *B.* Alas for our lot. *A.* Upon them two charioteers were placed: Leisure and Excess. <note>original: "crapula"; specifically the sickness, headache, or "hangover" resulting from over-indulgence in food and drink.</note> *B.* Ah, what an unfair fate. *A.* Two others were added to goad them on: Flattery and Custom. *B.* Troublesome indeed. *A.* Now Vanity herself was carried high in a chariot; it was marvelous what a face, what attire and adornment she had. *B.* You describe her in vain, for she is composed of all the particles of the earth, and moreover she is changeable every hour. *A.* But she also had two companions, or rather evil sisters: Impiety and Extravagance. *B.* Unfortunate plagues of the world. *A.* Subse- <meta>catchword: "subse-", likely continuing "subsequebantur" (followed after).</meta>

## 56. RESTORATION TO THE
## ORIGINAL STATE.
<note>original: "Restitutio in Integrum"; a legal term meaning the restoration of a person or state to their original legal condition, often used here as a metaphor for political or moral renewal.</note>

**A.** Ha! What is this gathering of people? What is this noise of people applauding? **B.** Ah! You alone will be unaware that we possess the <term>Public Good</term> <note>original: "Publicum Bonum"; the commonweal or general welfare of the community.</note>. **A.** I offer my congratulations, even though I am ignorant of these matters; but will you not bless me with a description of this new happiness? **B.** Why not rather accompany me, so that we may both adore this earthly deity? **A.** Tell me, please, who is that Goddess? **B.** I can scarcely speak for joy; she has been expected by us for so long, and having been summoned at last by our prayers, she has appeared. **A.** Is it Integrity? **B.** It is not she alone, but one who has brought Integrity along with a numerous choir of other virtues. **A.** O happy times! **B.** Happy indeed, in which a new <term>Hercules</term> <note>The mythical hero known for destroying monsters; here he represents a leader who cleanses the state of "monstrous" corruption.</note>, the tamer of all monsters, has appeared. **A.** You are killing me with this delay! **B.** A new Asclepiades, a new <term>Machaon</term> <note>In Greek mythology, Asclepius (Asclepiades) and his son Machaon were the legendary fathers of medicine; their arrival signifies the healing of the "diseased" state.</note> has been restored to the earth, sent to drive away our diseases. **A.** Free me...

### RESTORATION

**B.** And the empire has been restored to **Saturn** <note>Saturn was a mythical Roman god whose reign was considered a "Golden Age" of peace and abundance; B is claiming that this new era brings back that legendary perfection.</note>, to be recalled to its former happiness. **A.** Indeed, let us look at it then. **B.** Wait, you will receive her name in a moment, but first take off your cap. **A.** And my shoes, too, if you wish. **B.** May it be happy and auspicious: **Reformation** has entered our city with great pomp. **A.** Ha ha ha he he! **B.** May the gods destroy you, you who laugh at this most sacred name! **A.** Woe, woe, woe to us. **B.** Now are you crying? **A.** What should I do, if I am allowed neither to laugh nor to cry? **B.** Rather, you should marvel at our lot, we who have happened upon these times where all things are being <term>restored to their original state</term> <note>original: "in integrum restituentur"; a legal phrase meaning to return something to its exact original condition, as if a contract or injury never occurred.</note>. **A.** So, you are announcing new **baths** <note>original: "termas"; A is mockingly suggesting that "restoration" is nothing more than a new spa or medicinal spring.</note> to me, and medicated waters to cure all evils. **B.** Oh, if only you had seen the retinue of **Reformation**, you would not be mocking her now. **A.** I beg you, grant this much to my disbelief: describe her, and perhaps by doing so you might convert me. **B.** A single day is not enough, but know that among the most notable in her company were **Religion**, **Justice**, **Health**, **Knowledge**, **Labor**, **Reason**, **Honesty**, **Order**, and **Moderation**, besides countless other ornaments and supports of human life. **A.** You speak magnificently, truly; but is this Goddess of ours, **Reformation**, actually human and approachable?
