## 57. SALARY.

**A.** Are you always hungry? **B.** So it is fitting. **A.** Surely you must have provoked your Master’s servants at some point. **B.** To even beg is to provoke. **A.** And so they are pitiless, and hardly the sort of people who would ever be counted among the number of the Gods. **B.** Certainly, these household gods <term>Penates</term> <note>original: "Peneti"; the Roman spirits of the pantry and household, here used to refer to those who control the food supply.</note> of mine are completely deaf. **A.** Don't you know that the balance between labor and salary <term>salarium</term> <note>original: "salarium"; historically "salt-money," an allowance given to Roman soldiers to buy salt, which eventually became a general term for wages.</note> is most skillfully weighed, and no one is easily wronged? **B.** Is that so? While the labor nearly makes me slip, the salary only supplies me with salt. <note>The speaker is punning on the Latin "labor" (work) vs. "labi" (to slip) and "salarium" (salary) vs. "sal" (salt), suggesting his pay is meager.</note> **A.** Thus it is believable that you are both impatient with work and a seeker of luxuries. **B.** Certainly! For if anyone looks into my study, they find cushions everywhere; and if they look into my kitchen, they find the livers of parrotfish, the brains of pheasants and peacocks, flamingo tongues, and the milt of moray eels <note>These were famously expensive and exotic delicacies in Ancient Rome; Character B is sarcastically listing them to contrast with his actual poverty.</note> all mixed together. **A.** You are joking, surely. Yet I don't understand how others take good care of their hides <note>To "care for the hide" or skin was a common idiom for living a life of leisure and good eating.</note>, while you always display your hunger. **B.** Because I have nothing except my salary. **A.** Does it really become so thin, while in the meantime they have a bad reputation among the common people? **B.** There is great inequality, but also irregularity. Regarding this, I assure you: I would rather live on a fixed amount of porridge, however modest, than on such a pittance over three hundred and sixty [days]...

### SALARY.

...to distribute five days. **A.** Bah, poor Arithmetic! But why are you fed so unequally? **B.** Naturally, because hay is given to the ox, and sugar to the parrot. **A.** And the colts who work the land are fed on chaff, while the horses that lounge about are fattened with oats. **B.** And those who make shoes for others run about barefoot. **A.** Is it a matter of luck, or of one’s way of life, to live more sumptuously? **B.** Formerly it was luck, but now it depends on the way of life; for the more useless and base the art one has learned, the more generously he is fed today. For he who has learned to fold napkins, or carve a goose, or turn a dog <note>likely a "turnspit dog," a breed used to turn meat over a fire</note>, or paint a Thais <note>original: "Thaidem"; a famous Athenian courtesan, here used to mean a common prostitute</note>, or blow a flute, or juggle fire, or spray water, or string pearls, or curl hair, or scrub pimples, is hired for five hundred, and even a thousand crowns <term>coronatis</term>. Yet he who is God’s interpreter on earth [the clergy], who keeps watch over the fatherland, who puts blood and life at risk, can scarcely snatch a hundred and fifty florins <term>florenos</term> <note>The author is contrasting the high pay of entertainers and domestic servants with the meager stipends of scholars, soldiers, and priests.</note> from the pincers of the administrators. **A.** Where then are those Magnificent Patrons and most generous Maecenases <term>mœcenates</term> <note>original: "mœcenates"; named after Gaius Maecenas, the Roman patron of Virgil and Horace; a term for wealthy sponsors of the arts.</note> whom you place at the front of all your papers? Where is that generosity toward letters, that eternal provision for the arts, that sacred trade in virtues? **B.** These are the delusions of the ancients; today life is lived differently. **A.** But what about those who sit at the helm <note>original: "ad clavos sedent"; literally "those at the tillers," referring to those in government</note>, who are not ignorant of literature—do they not intervene or promote anything? **B.** Not at all. For as each man sits comfortably, he knows the tricks by which he got there; anyone who believes he rose through scholarship is a fool. Some accidental, and usually ridiculous, chance has elevated many. **A.** So, will you grant nothing to your "little letters" <note>studies or scholarship</note> from now on? **B.** Absolutely nothing.

### § 8 DIGRESSION.

**A.** Where have you been, where are you from? **B.** From Europe. **A.** What strange thing is this? Is "Europe" some city? **B.** To me indeed it now seems so, however much it [lies open], and is intersected by rivers, and distinguished by mountains and [plains]. For I have surveyed all its inhabitants, like the various citizens of [a single] marketplace. **A.** Have you surveyed Europe in such a short time, while I have not yet inspected my own house from all sides? **B.** Oh, you have eyes of stone and the body of a tortoise! [I] would compete with the birds in speed. **A.** Tell [me then] which citizens of your "city" of Europe you have seen. **B.** Ah! Why will you weary me? I have seen *Spaniards*, *Frenchmen*, [*It]alians*, *Hungarians*, *Bohemians*, *Poles*, *Russians*, *Swe[d]es*, *Danes*, *Englishmen*, *Scots*, and *Germans*. **A.** And [all] these in no more than the three years during which you seemed to [me] to be absent? **B.** Nay, a little less. **A.** [Therefore] you must have run through those lands. **B.** Rather [flown] through them, for I mostly used **Pegasean couriers** <note>original: "veredis pegaſeis"; a reference to the winged horse Pegasus, meaning he used the fastest possible postal relays or messenger horses</note>. **A.** But a little while ago you said you "surveyed" them; you should have said you "wandered through" them. **B.** You are quibbling. **A.** How indeed did you speak to so many people, being unskilled in [their] languages? **B.** Through an interpreter: for the one who [hired] me has long been most skilled in both roads and languages. **A.** But you, while you [looked] out at foreign things as if mute, what pleasure did you have? **B.** Bah, [how] simple you are! Is it not pleasant [to see] so many cit[ies]... <meta>catchword: bes (likely "urbes," meaning cities)</meta>

[...cities] <note>The Latin text begins with "bes," likely the end of "urbes" (cities), continuing from the previous page's list of things seen.</note>, so many rivers, so many faces, so many styles of clothing, so many kinds of food and wine, so many species of animals and trees to contemplate, and to gaze upon the public comedy, as it were, of the world. **A.** I am almost convinced: for while others dream at night, you are already able to dream during the day through the memory of such a pleasant spectacle. **B.** You trifler! <header>ON SPEAKING GREEK.</header>

...you are being unfair. **B.** I indeed cannot sufficiently admire the Greek language as the mother and storehouse of wisdom, but I am constantly angry with you and your kind, who disgrace both languages with such foolish mixing. **A.** Is it not **with the flavoring** <note>original: τῷ χρίσματι; literally "the anointing" or "oil," used here metaphorically for seasoning speech</note>, that is, the refinement of the Greeks, **in the word** <note>original: τῷ λόγῳ</note>? **B.** What a flea is in the ear, that is what the rattling together of Latin and Greek is. You don't seem to know that it is one thing to adorn a speech with Greek maxims—especially the rarer ones—but quite another to mix the vocabulary of different languages together. The former is the mark of the learned; the latter is for the insane. **A.** **Do not mock me** <note>original: σὺ μὴ σκώπτεις</note>, for I know what befits a man of letters; **pay no attention** <note>original: ἀμέλησον</note>, you barbarian! **B.** Don't you notice how tastelessly you speak? **A.** If indeed we believe your **ears** <note>original: ὤταις</note>. **B.** Hah! You’re making that noise again. **A.** I can certainly speak either one **separately** <note>original: χωρὶς</note>, if I like. **B.** Try it, I pray, to see if you can. **A.** **Easily** <note>original: εὐχερῶς</note>. **B.** Watch out for yourself. **A.** But if Latin should fail me, you won't forbid **borrowed words** <note>original: τὰς δανεισιὰς λέξεις</note>. **B.** Oh, the violence of habit! But what if someone else mixed German words with Latin in this same way? **A.** **Truly** <note>original: ἀληθῶς</note>, even that isn't always done badly. **B.** I suspected you would approve, for both habits flow from the same spring. But what do you think of those <term>Frenchified</term> <note>original: Galliatis; a pejorative term for those mimicking French manners or speech</note> fellows of ours, as I might call them, or the <term>Italianized</term> <note>original: Italionatis</note> ones, for whom our mother tongue seems narrow and poor on all sides? **A.** The **judgment of the gods** <note>original: τῶν θεῶν κρίσις</note> has not yet received them. **B.** But custom supports them most uncontrollably. But let us put aside that foolishness. **A.** You mean the <term>foreign-madness</term> <note>original: ξενομανίαν (xenomania); an obsessive preference for foreign things, especially languages</note>. **B.** Come, let it be so; let us pass over it, I say. Haven't you noticed in our literary crowd those who, when they ought to speak in German, speak in Latin...

<header>ON GREEK AFFECTATION</header>

...they are constantly making a noise, but when it comes to Latin, they are silent, or they babble as if the rules of grammar died with **Priscian** <note>original: *Prisciani interitu*; Priscian was the most influential Latin grammarian of late antiquity; to "break Priscian's head" was a common idiom for speaking poor Latin.</note>. I think the same judgment applies to those who **affect a Greek style** <note>original: *Graecissantibus*</note>, and perhaps they are even more ignorant. We might compare them to those traveling peddlers—or to use a Greek term, **charlatans** <note>original: *agyrtis*</note>—who have a few Latin medical terms ready for use, which they ring in the ears of simple country folk.

**A.** **I knew this long ago** <note>original: τοῦτο καὶ πάλαι ἠπιστάμην</note>. But let us not pass judgment on everyone, or at least not on many. **B.** I judge many boldly, and even most, if you can bear it. For those who are truly learned in Greek use each language distinctly at different times, or mix them with true elegance.

**A.** I should like to hear from you the **proposition, the exposition, the definition, the construction, the proof, and the conclusion** <note>original: *πρότασιν, ἔκθεσιν, διορισμὸν, κατασκευὴν, ἀπόδειξιν, & συμπέρασμα*</note> of this matter.

**B.** Ha ha he! If you say "The School," you have said everything. For where so many technical terms are born, there also arises a disordered use of them. For what does not happen where a man is considered more learned simply because he speaks in pure jargon? It is as if a cobbler were considered better because he talks of his awl, his thread, his pitch, or his leather-cutting tool.

**A.** **Hush, speak words of good omen!** <note>original: σιώπα, εὐφήμει; a classical formula used to avoid bad luck or divine anger</note> **For it is not safe for you to say, nor for me to hear such things** <note>original: οὐ γὰρ ἀσφαλές ἐστι σοὶ λέγειν, οὔτε ἐμοὶ ἀκούειν τὰ τοιαῦτα</note>.

# CRIMINALS

...strips them of their clothes, or one who is too watchful, because he arranges the household vessels by night. <note>This opening fragment appears to describe the behavior of a thief or a deceptive servant.</note> **A.** Ah, those wretched ones, for whom alone sinning comes at a high price; but truly, how do you comfort them?

**B.** First, I rebuke them most harshly—those who have dared to do a thing contrary to nature and all human laws, who have spent their lives in wretched idleness and ruinous license, who have had no care for religion or civic virtues, who have fed upon the labor and sweat of others, who have trampled upon both the advice and the examples of their parents and all good men, and whatever other things come to mind by which hearts are melted; then, I raise them up toward serious **repentance** <note>original: *pœnitentiam*</note> and an ardent imploring of **Divine mercy** <note>original: *misericordiae Divinae*</note>; finally, I prepare them to undergo death patiently and bravely.

**A.** All this is truly excellent, and I wish that your care for souls were extended to many, and indeed to very many more.

**B.** Ha! Would you then want there to be *more* **criminals** <note>original: *maleficos*; this term refers specifically to those who do evil or commit crimes, often used in a legal context.</note>?

**A.** By no means; I wish rather that there were fewer, through your diligence. But are there not also infinite criminals who nevertheless wear various ornaments of virtue instead of chains?

**B.** Who are those?

**A.** Those **Giants** <note>original: *Gigantes*; a classical and biblical allusion to prideful, powerful men who rebel against the divine order.</note> (you know the ones I mean) who perpetually blaspheme the name of God through myriads of **Oaths** <note>original: *Sacramentorum*; here likely referring to the swearing of sacred oaths in a profane or deceptive manner.</note> and every holy aspect of the **Passion** <note>original: *Passionis*; the suffering of Christ.</note>; who give whole years to gluttony and drunkenness; who pollute homes indiscriminately with foul lust; who insult the helpless and gnaw the poor down to the very marrow; who laugh at religion and civil laws over their cups and drag them into the filthiest talk; who, by the foulness of their mouths, are a burden everywhere to decent ears; who within two years or sooner grow rich despite such extravagance, and compete with the diligence of the most hardworking; who most clearly [waste] time...

# CRIMINALS

...they burn the debt owed to God and to our soul. Those who oppose all good things—and if there are any other "talents" belonging to these monsters—do you not rebuke them harshly and sharpen your tongue against such pestilential behaviors?

**B.** I certainly do so vigorously from the **pulpit** <note>original: *è suggestu*; this confirms that Speaker B is a member of the clergy or a preacher.</note>; let the **Magistrates** <note>The secular legal authorities, as opposed to the church.</note> see to the rest.

**B.** I cannot deny it.

**A.** At least those should be corrected.

**B.** They do not bend; they are so accustomed to being wicked. Yet, they are more manageable when they are with me.

**A.** Naturally—so that when they have mumbled "I, a miserable sinner" in passing, you might more easily add: "Have faith, son, your sins are forgiven you."

**B.** Let us leave the judgment to God.

**A.** Meanwhile, you rage against the poor wretches.

**B.** What will happen if they are allowed to steal with impunity?

**A.** And what of it while *these* men plunder, infect, and contaminate entire cities? ### 61. THE EXPECTANT ONE

**A.** What do those bandages around your neck mean? Do you have **Demosthenes’ disease** <note>original: *Demosthenis morbum*; a historical joke referring to the Greek orator Demosthenes, who once wrapped his neck in bandages and claimed to have a "silver squinsy" (a sore throat) to avoid speaking in the assembly after accepting a bribe.</note>?

**B.** It is easy to laugh at a miserable man.

**A.** I will sympathize, then, as soon as you reveal this ailment to me.

**B.** It does not yet have a name, but I know not how my neck is growing stiff against my shoulders.

**A.** You are indeed unfortunate, but what do you suspect caused it?

**B.** I would believe it to be frequent **looking upward** <note>original: *suspicionem*; here the author uses a pun on the Latin word *suspicio*, which means both "suspicion" and the literal act of "looking up at something."</note>.

**A.** Toward heaven? You are far too devoted.

**B.** Now indeed I look toward heaven, since there is no help to be found among men.

**A.** So you were looking up to men?

**B.** It must be confessed—and for a long time.

**A.** What were you expecting, then?

**B.** That those high-and-mighty men would eventually lift me out of the dust and mud and [place me] in a more comfortable spot...

...they might replace. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, concluding a thought from the previous page.</note> **A.** What is the matter? **B.** While I continually strain at the **wheel of honors and offices** <note>original: *honorum & officiorum rotam*; a metaphor for the fickle Wheel of Fortune, specifically regarding social and political climbing</note>, and strike against such inexorable ears with my petitions, the wheel turns; those whom I had already nearly persuaded, it lifts higher, and immediately throws new people in my way. Thus, I have had to cry out to those elevated ones, while simultaneously trying to win over these newer arrivals. I am even nauseated and ready to vomit; for who would not be weary of a decade consumed in vain by petitions? **A.** Have faith; our Christ is more easily moved by prayer. **B.** But is it truly permitted to ask? For in that *other* heaven, the rule is: he who asks is considered base, and he who remains silent remains hidden. **A.** Christ is different; you will never tire Him with prayers, and you will never be obscure to Him in any corner. **B.** But does He also have a **tablet of expectants** <note>original: *tabulam expectantiam*; in the legal language of the Church, an "expectative" was a document promising a person the next vacant position or "living." **Technical Vocabulary:**
*   **Court:** The administrative and social circle surrounding a prince or the Pope.
*   **Christ:** The central figure of Christian faith, contrasted here as a more merciful "Patron."
*   **Horoscope:** A map of the stars at birth, believed to determine one's fate.
*   **Weariness (Tædium):** A deep, spiritual boredom or exhaustion.
*   **Wheel:** The "Wheel of Fortune" which raises people up and casts them down.

## 62. THE HOROSCOPE.

**A.** Is there then so little goodwill, so little fairness toward me in the stars? **B.** Why are you so vexed? **A.** I beg you, join me, so that we may be angry at the heavens. **B.** Angry at the heavens? **A.** Certainly, because it carries stars so inauspicious for us. **B.** I indeed long ago learned to ignore all stars, except for that one **star of Jacob**. <note>A reference to Numbers 24:17, "a star shall come out of Jacob," traditionally interpreted by Christians as a prophecy of the birth of Jesus.</note> **A.** It is easy to ignore them if they would keep away from us and leave our lives more tolerable. **B.** And so you believe the bitternesses of our life come from the stars? **A.** So they say, those who scan the whole sky. <note>He refers to astrologers, who were often consulted for career and health advice during this period.</note> **B.** But others deny it, and the stars are not angry at them for the denial, nor do they send punishments upon them. **A.** O, they are far too happy! Are the stars specifically cursed and angry at me? **B.** Have you looked so closely at your whole **horoscope** <note>original: *horoscopum*; a map of the heavens at the moment of birth used to predict a person's character and fate</note> that no good fortune could possibly be hidden anywhere? **A.** No hope remains, unless I end this unlucky life as soon as possible. **B.** But if the heavens turned by your will, what would you command the **Planets**? <note>In the Ptolemaic system, the planets were believed to exert direct physical and spiritual influence on earthly affairs.</note> For I hear the rule of the world is chiefly entrusted to them. **A.** Ah, why do you ask? **Saturn** would win over craftsmen for me; **Jupiter** ♃ would bring me Princes; **Mars** ♂, Nobles; the **Sun** ☉, the Wealthy; **Venus** ♀, Women; **Mercury** ☿, the Learned; the **Moon** ☽...

## 63. HESITATION.

**A.** Why is it that I always see you in such a state—that is, as a "nobody"—at an age when you ought to be serving God and the State? 

**B.** Because all things are more difficult than anyone can put into words. 

**A.** Stop being a human then, for whom this is the supreme law: to labor. 

**B.** And yet, there are degrees and weights to these labors; while I examine and compare them among themselves, time flows away.

**B.** It has too much austerity, and too much danger. <note>likely referring to the risk of heresy or the heavy moral responsibility.</note>

For what need is there that the labors of all men should afflict you, when a single one could occupy your time—if only you could believe you could endure it? ## 64. THE EXILE.

<margin>A.</margin> Most distinguished sir, since our God has so arranged things that I am currently in need while you live comfortably and with dignity, you will not take it amiss if I reverently seek from you some relief for my poverty—as much as your kindness <note>original: *humanitas*—this refers to the shared feeling of being human and the kindness expected between civilized people</note> might persuade you and your financial situation allow. And I ask this for the sake of our shared Christ, whose name I have counted dear even to the point of risking my life and losing my possessions; for the sake of our common fatherland, for which I have faithfully exposed this body of mine, such as it is; for the sake of the learning <note>original: *literas*—referring to their shared classical education or "letters," a common bond among scholars</note> familiar to us both, which I hope might intercede on my behalf with you; and finally, for the sake of the various turns of human fortune, which even the most fortunate man fears. So may God wish you to be safe and flourishing, and recognize and crown you as a benefactor to His members <note>referring to the "members of the body of Christ," a common metaphor for fellow believers in need</note>.

<margin>B.</margin> It truly pains me, my dear man, that good people should suffer, and anyone who endures injury calls me to heartfelt sympathy. Indeed, if someone even hungers for Christ's sake, I must certainly feed him, even if our shared Fatherland required nothing at all, or kindness did not persuade me. Meanwhile, do not be angry with me if I modestly and candidly ask for some witnesses to that exile of yours, so that by their agreement your integrity might shine more brightly. For you cannot be unaware that there is a certain class of men, harmful to God and good people alike, who attach the sacred name of *Exile* to their own idleness, wandering, and even wickedness, and thus prey upon the sympathy of good men.

<margin>A.</margin> I praise...

# FAITH.
<note>original: *Fides*—in this context, the title refers both to the religious faith of the exile and the "good faith" or credibility of the documents he provides</note>

Indeed, distinguished sir, I appreciate that concern of yours. Here are letters <note>referring to formal letters of recommendation or testimonials from other scholars and officials</note> by which you will be more certain that all my possessions were once spent for the sake of God, and that nothing remains of me except this frail frame—but it is a frame no less devoted to the Gospel, should any Prince desire a Church or a school to be entrusted to it. **B.** There is enough credibility in these letters, and I do not doubt that they have satisfied others as well, wherever you have presented them. **A.** I will never be able to convince you, excellent man, how harsh most people are, how difficult, and how suspicious—though I would rather attribute that to the behavior of those who are impostors. **B.** It is truly not right to be so distrustful that we completely strip away Christian charity, especially since we give to Christ—in whose name the request is made—and not to impostors. **A.** We are such creatures that we hope for the best from the wealthy, yet we fear every possible worst thing from the poor. **B.** But what about the Princes, and those who have a public treasury <term>fiscus|a state or royal treasury</term> dedicated to this purpose? **A.** Alms are given, but beyond that, there is no other comfort. **B.** And the same is done for trumpeters, actors, and musicians—and not infrequently more generously. I would actually wish that some kind of stipend for exiles be established, where those known for certain to have been faithful to Christ, even to the point of shedding blood, might be supported; this would be while their life is still vigorous enough to be applied to further service for Christ, or as it grows more faint, so that it might end more comfortably. **A.** That would be considered a massive expense. **B.** Perhaps you do not know how much we waste on dogs. But now, come inside with me.

-> MOROPROT. <-

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 125. Character B is expanding on his argument that "Truth" is not a singular, simple thing, but rather "manifold" or multifaceted, depending on the context and the spirit in which it is spoken. He uses the concept of being called a "fool" to illustrate how the same factual statement can serve different moral purposes.</meta>

<page-num>126</page-num>

<header>-> TRUTH. <-</header>

If some people wanted to declare us fools, that would undoubtedly be true, but each would understand it in a different way. ***A.*** Please see if you can make me out to be a fool several times over, and in different ways. ***B.*** Very easily—both in a bad way and a good one. ***A.*** Let us hear it. ***B.*** Imagine if some Julian <note>original: *Iulianus*—referring to Julian the Apostate, the Roman Emperor who opposed Christianity</note> calls you a fool because you neglect the present life for the sake of the future; you accept this title, which Paul <note>Saint Paul the Apostle, who wrote of being a "fool for Christ"</note> says is honorable and precious to God. Has not the former spoken truly in an impious way, while the latter has spoken truly in a pious way?

Now, if some arrogant person reproaches you for your current lack of resources, and a Christian boasts of your poverty, both have spoken truly and described an "earthly fool," but with a different intention <note>original: *affectu*—referring to the speaker's inner disposition or state of mind</note>. Furthermore, if someone Envious <note>original: *Lividus*—personifying envy</note> notes a defect in your intellect, while a just man modestly warns you of your flaws <note>original: *nævis*—literally "birthmarks" or "blemishes"</note>, you have once again been made a fool twice over by two different truth-tellers. Finally, if some buffoon <note>original: *scurra*</note> shamefully slanders you, and another witty person mockingly critiques you, you will be a fool under both a bitter truth and a savory one.

I add nothing more, for it is enough to show that truth can be one thing when it is impious—such as that of Satan when he opposes sinners—and another when it is pious—such as that of the Church whenever she calls back those who wander. There is another "permitted" truth, such as that of the carping critics <note>original: *momorum*—referring to Momus, the Greek god of mockery and blame</note>, the Zoili <note>Zoilus was a Greek grammarian famous for his harsh, nitpicking criticism of Homer</note>, and fanatics, who delight solely in the errors of men. There is another human truth, such as that of those who contribute their labors and most skillful investigations to the commonwealth. There is another arrogant truth, such as the **Aristotelian** kind, which battles with all other opinions and strives for dominion; another is modest, such as the **Christian** kind, in which revealed things are guarded by simple faith and propagated with a humble voice. ## 72. THE UNLEARNED <note>original: *Idiota*—In this context, it refers to a layperson or someone without formal academic schooling, rather than its modern derogatory meaning</note>

<margin>A.</margin> How wretched a thing it is not to know. **B.** And so Socrates was the most wretched of all, who knew only this one thing: that he knew nothing. **A.** He, however, was only feigning ignorance, when in truth he was the most knowledgeable of all the philosophers. **B.** I, on the contrary, would believe he seriously acknowledged both his own ignorance and that of others. For although he had penetrated nearly all human knowledge, he saw that he did not yet properly grasp how to know, or how to be wise, since most of us do not know what—or how much—we ought to know. **A.** Beware saying this of our age, in which we have reached the very peaks of all arts and sciences. Nothing remains, except that we might even teach Metaphysics <note>original: *Methaphisica*—the branch of philosophy dealing with the first principles of things, including abstract concepts such as being, knowing, and time; considered the most difficult subject in the curriculum</note> to our boys, or even our maidservants...

<header>MONASTERIES.</header>

...and that the nobility rightfully reclaim what was snatched from the people by fraud. 
*A.* Let them reclaim it, certainly. But what portion of it returns to the subjects, or to the heirs of those simple folk? Instead, it passes into the hands of strangers, is wasted by foreign extravagance, and the wealth of the country is plainly carried away by the hands of others. Meanwhile, the people themselves are in need: the poor lack the <term>alms</term> <note>original: *Eleemosyna*—charitable relief and food once provided by monastic houses</note> of the monks, and the youth are forgotten among those ruins and wildernesses. Finally, this wine, grain, and income—whatever was once devoted to God and religion—is now consumed in a way that is neither sacred nor devoted. Two things must follow from this: the wrath of God and the poverty of the people. This is on top of the insults of our enemies; we try to dodge their words with accusations of their own luxury, rather than proving them wrong through a holy and religious management of these most sacred assets. 

*B.* As long as our own religious men do not go hungry, and nothing is lacking for religion and education, and the beggars have their places of refuge, what need is there to poke into others' business? 

*A.* And yet, there are many places where Christ and the Church are in want—places where those resources were owed. Instead, you throw them to the dogs, or elsewhere to oxen, or elsewhere to pigs, or they are stuffed and swallowed at the "altars of the belly" dedicated to the providers and priests of Volupia, Stimula, Rumina, Edulica, Potina, and Mellona. <note>A list of minor Roman deities associated with physical indulgence: Volupia (pleasure), Stimula (passion/goading), Rumina (nursing), Edulica (eating), Potina (drinking), and Mellona (honey).</note>

# 76. THE STUDENT.

*A.* Is this how you alone idle about while we work?
*B.* Naturally, for these are my holidays.
*A.* Oh? Do you have any holidays other than annual ones? For I never see any traces of your labor.
*B.* The work is done within, and it is the exhaustion of this brain, to which a formal vocation <note>original: *vocatio*—referring to his calling or professional status as a student</note> has now been granted.
*A.* What you are manufacturing in that brain is certainly not clear; however, I do know how much your mouth and throat are free for frequent drinking parties.
*B.* That is typical of you unrefined people, who, ignorant of the value of letters <note>original: *literarum*—humanistic learning and literature</note>, compare them to a few paltry coins.
*A.* Why do you speak of "paltry coins" when those "letters" of yours devour entire loads of money? <note>original: *aeris sarcinas*—literally "bundles of bronze," referring to heavy financial costs</note>
*B.* "Mine," you say? In the entire University, there is nothing more frugal or even more meager.
*A.* Can you bear it if I itemize that "meagerness" of yours?
*B.* Gladly, so that my thriftiness may be clear to both you and others.
*A.* Come then, recite what you spend.
*B.* Very well: for annual room and board <term>commons</term> <note>original: *convictu*—the shared living and dining arrangements at a university</note>, note 78 <term>florins</term> <note>original: *fl.*—the florin was a standard gold coin of significant value</note>; figure a florin and a half per week.
*A.* I have noted it.
*B.* Extra expenses, however, run to 52 florins—that is, one florin per week.
*A.* What is the meaning of this?
*B.* If anything is spent beyond the fixed allowance, whether for the sake of honor, or guests, or even thirst, or visitors.
*A.* I have noted it nonetheless.
*B.* Now for my outfitting <note>original: *investitū*—clothing and personal equipment</note>, let me spend no less than 40 florins; and besides that, I will give 6 florins to the Tailor and 6 florins to the Shoemaker.
*A.* Heaven help us! If these seem like "minimal" amounts to you... but go on.
*B.* For books and the <term>bookbinder</term> <note>original: *bibliopœga*</note>, surely you will permit 30 florins, if I include paper, pens, and ink?
*A.* Since you force me to do so.
*B.* Then the honorariums for the Teachers <note>original: *Præceptoribus*</note>...

*A.* Therefore, you have need of one thousand five hundred florins.

*A.* Nor have I indicated to you how slowly and wretchedly fifteen hundred florins are collected.
*B.* Nor have I indicated to you the great price at which the treasure of arts and letters is sold.
*A.* Nor have I indicated to you how lazy and illiterate we find you people to be immediately afterward.

# 77. GREENNESS.

<margin>A.</margin> How often do I catch you walking around here, muttering I know not what to the earth? 
**B.** Ah! There is nothing that delights me as much.
**A.** Do these herbs, shrubs, and trees actually answer you? 
**B.** Many things indeed, and excellent ones; for this is the alphabet of God, whose artistry <note>original: *picturam*—literally "painting" or "picture," referring to the visual beauty of creation</note> anyone who recognizes it is never weary of reading. 
**A.** Do you have different eyes than I do then? 
**B.** I do not doubt it; otherwise, the most elegant contemplation of this vast book would have possessed you entirely long ago. 
**A.** I do not understand that unusual literacy <note>original: *literaturam*—meaning the ability to "read" nature as one reads a book</note> of yours. 
**B.** Look here for me at four types of evergreens: the Laurel, the olive, the boxwood, and the palm. 
**A.** What of it? Let them be green, for all I care. 
**B.** Even a beast <note>original: *pecus*—a term for someone unlearned or lacking spiritual perception</note> would at least be delighted by it, if nothing else. 
**A.** Fine, it delights me. 
**B.** And does an admiration for that <term>viridity</term> <note>original: *viroris*—the freshness, vigor, or green color of plants</note> come over you? 
**A.** I wonder at it. 
**B.** And curiosity about the cause stimulates you? 
**A.** I am stimulated. 
**B.** I shall tell you what it seems to the <term>natural philosophers</term> <note>original: *Physicis*—scholars who studied the physical world and the properties of nature</note>: that the Laurel is of a very hot temperament <note>original: *complexionis*—referring to the theory of humors and qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) applied to plants</note>, and excludes all cold, and thus it stays green. That the olive always waters its roots with a full sap <note>original: *succiplenā*</note>, and from there always nourishes the same branches. That the dense boxwood never lets go of the power of greenness it has once possessed. But that the palm is of a most temperate nature, which produces and preserves its leaves through the moisture of the sea. 
**A.** I hear you, and I believe you, but what use is that to me, or what "divine alphabet" are you showing me? 
**B.** Are you such a blockhead <note>original: *stipes*—literally a log or post, used as a common insult for a dull-witted person</note> that <insert>s</insert> the Laurel [reminds] you of the prosperity of the wicked—

# GREENNESS.

The Olive of heavenly protection (Psalm 52). The Palm of righteous beauty (Psalm 92). Does it not remind one, or indeed rouse one toward that perennial and immobile <term>viridity</term> <note>original: *viriditatem*—the greenness, vigor, and spiritual freshness of the soul</note> of a good man? For what can a man learn on this earth more elegant or sublime than how to remain unconquered among so many human attacks, immutable among so many changes, and immobile among so many shocks? Or, to speak more plainly, how to appear always green amidst the frosts and snows of this <note>The author likely refers to the "final age" of the world, a common historical trope suggesting the world was in its declining, wintry years.</note> final age. 

<margin>A.</margin> And will the boxwood, or the olive, really teach that? 

<margin>B.</margin> Certainly; for just as the Laurel reminds you of excellent reason, so the olive suggests a just liberality, the Boxwood commends a strong constancy, and the Palm provides a blend of temperance. This <term>chariot of virtues</term> <note>original: *virtutum quadriga*—a classical metaphor comparing a set of four virtues to a four-horse team pulling a chariot</note> will surely never fail to carry one toward the stability of a blessed and ever-green tranquility. 

<margin>A.</margin> Who would believe your laurel or your palm intended such things for itself, unless one were to divine it along with you? 

<margin>B.</margin> Indeed, and many other things as well; for the more attentively we gaze upon the <term>signatures of creatures</term> <note>original: *creaturarum signaturas*—the "Doctrine of Signatures," the belief that God marked every living thing with a physical sign of its hidden purpose or spiritual meaning</note>, the more deeply we are immersed in Divine Wisdom. 

<margin>A.</margin> O, how happy you are, for whom there is a double delight in things: one earthly, the other heavenly! 

<margin>B.</margin> Rather, it is a manifold delight. But while you laugh and remain unrefined, it appears you are no different from a beast which, when set among flowers and painted grass, takes pleasure in neither its eyes nor its nose, but instead tramples some things and grazes upon others.

# 78. THE CORRECTION OF TIME.

<margin>A.</margin> Let us correct ourselves for the better. <note>original: *Emendemus in melius*</note>

<margin>B.</margin> What are you humming there?

<margin>A.</margin> Why are you lurking? I was here by myself.

<margin>B.</margin> Were you with a good man? <note>A classical joke: "I am never less alone than when alone," implying one is in the company of one's own good character.</note>

<margin>A.</margin> Believe me, for who would be so wicked as to dare deny it? Indeed, that song came to my mind not without reason.

<margin>B.</margin> Were you correcting something in yourself?

<margin>A.</margin> Not just in me, by Pollux, <note>original: *ædepol*—a common Roman oath</note> but however much time flows by irregularly.

<margin>B.</margin> Does that Phoenix, Scaliger, <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), whose work *De emendatione temporum* revolutionized the study of historical chronology.</note> offer no help with the **correction of time**?

<margin>A.</margin> He is of little use for this.

<margin>B.</margin> Then let Suslega <note>Likely referring to a contemporary chronologist or astronomer.</note> add a four-year period, or the most ingenious Kepler <note>Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), the famous astronomer who also wrote on the year of Christ's birth.</note> add five years.

<margin>A.</margin> I desire different calculations.

<margin>B.</margin> Perhaps the "Calculator" himself, Swineshead, <note>original: *Suisset*—Richard Swineshead, a 14th-century English mathematician and logician known for such complexity he was called a "Gorgonian knot" for future scholars.</note> the Gordian knot of posterity?

<margin>A.</margin> I have nothing to do with him.

<margin>B.</margin> Do you wish for Brocard <note>James Brocard, a 16th-century mystical interpreter of the Apocalypse who predicted a coming "Sacred Empire."</note> to restore the age for you, or announce the Sacred Empire through him?

<margin>A.</margin> These things are above me.

<margin>B.</margin> Or do you perhaps expect a "correction of instruction" <note>original: *institutionis emendationem*</note> such as Hutter <note>Elias Hutter or Leonhard Hutter, prominent Lutheran scholars.</note> promised and Ratke <note>original: *Ratichius*—Wolfgang Ratke, an educational reformer.</note> exhibited?

<margin>A.</margin> Not even that helps here.

<margin>B.</margin> What about the admirable algebra of Viète <note>François Viète (1540–1603), the "father of modern algebra."</note> or the numbers of Faulhaber? <note>Johannes Faulhaber (1580–1635), a mathematician and occultist.</note> Will they dig out your deep secrets?

<margin>A.</margin> They obscure things more.

<margin>B.</margin> Perhaps you hope for the Spanish Monarchy, which the Jesuits dream of. <note>Referring to the *Monarchia Hispanica*, a contemporary geopolitical ideal of a universal Catholic empire under Spain.</note>

<margin>A.</margin> That is beyond the quaternary. <note>original: *quaternarium*—likely referring to a system of four world empires; A suggests his concern is of a different order entirely.</note>

<margin>B.</margin> I would not dare mention to you the expectation of the Jews, for whose Messiah all things are reserved to be corrected.

<margin>A.</margin> Away with it! My matter does not require such grand preparation.

<margin>B.</margin> Of what "time," then, do you desire the correction?

<margin>A.</margin> I will tell you, but with your kind <note>The page ends here; the catchword indicates the sentence continues: "with your kind permission."</note>

<margin>A.</margin> ...pardon, if perhaps you were once entangled in these snares.

Finally, whatever is anxiously devoted to the investigation of the future, to divinations, prognostics, horoscopes <note>original: *genituris*</note>, the Kabbalah, seals, and mystic numbers; for these, I would wish to have returned the years spent so poorly until now, to be passed hereafter in repentance, shame, and serious labors.

<margin>B.</margin> At least women should not have been omitted, for whom all their time is lost in the care of the body.

<margin>A.</margin> Rather, let us mourn the entire human race, which, in such a shortage of time and shortness of life, gives most of it to fables, trifles, and vanity—very little to itself, and almost nothing to God.

# THE NEW DISCOVERIES

<margin>A.</margin> ...stand forth.

<margin>B.</margin> Please do.

<margin>A.</margin> I will not just name the New World <note>The Americas</note>—once a great infamy for being unknown—from which medicine has been increased, astronomy reformed, and the number of known animals and plants of the earth amplified. <margin>B.</margin> If only all those things had not brought us infinite evils, and had not produced the slaughter of men everywhere! The New World even now is drenched in innocent blood. Chemistry is favorable to a few, but for many it is a capital crime. The sea transmits both goods and evils, and devours human bodies in great numbers. Printed letters darken, confuse, and distract the whole world. Cannons are the infernal things they are, born for human destruction. Clocks, which ought to remind us of the passing of time, instead leave us standing there yawning. Telescopes threaten us with I know not what kind of "inhabitants of the stars" <note>An early reference to the unsettling idea of extraterrestrial life or "plurality of worlds" sparked by telescopic observation</note>. Machines demand that men become the companions of their labor. Silkworms <note>original: *bombices*</note> are full...

...thousands serve a shameful vanity. ### 80. TELESCOPES <note>original: *Perspicilia*</note>

<margin>A.</margin> Look, an observer! <note>original: *speculatorem*—can also mean a scout or a spy.</note> 

<margin>B.</margin> Rather, a traitor, if you will.

## 81. FORTIFICATION.

*A.* Is it permitted to look into these papers? 

*B.* To no one, except a most trusted friend. 

*A.* I am as solid as stone if you wish, for not even the "little strings" <note>original: *fidiculae*—this term refers to small stringed instruments, but was also a common metaphor for the cords used in torture to extract secrets</note> could wrench your secrets from me.

*A.* And yet I see nothing but lines. 

*B.* Are you not skilled in these types of drawings? 

*A.* Not at all; therefore, take back these mysteries of yours. 

*B.* You must be instructed: you see here a <term>ground plan</term> <note>original: *ignographia*—a variation of *ichnographia*, the bird's-eye floor plan of a building</note> of some structure, then a <term>cross-section</term> <note>original: *sciographia*—a drawing showing the interior or profile of a building</note>, and finally an <term>elevation</term> <note>original: *orthographia*—a scaled drawing of the front or side facade</note>.

*A.* That is enough. 

*B.* Now these diagrams must be judged by the most ingenious architects, wherever they may be: Italians, Belgians, French, or Germans.

### FORTIFICATION.

...the first designer, or rather, which of the princes is going to build it.

*B.* Once again I call upon your loyalty, for the matter is entirely secret.

*A.* To trust too much or to distrust too much is equally a vice; speak out.

*B.* Hypocrisy is planning this rampart for herself, where she may hide safely and rule over men from behind a cover, just like the Abyssinian Emperors <note>original: *Abissini Imperatores*—historical accounts of Ethiopia (Abyssinia) often fascinated Europeans with tales of emperors who lived in extreme seclusion, ruling without being seen by their subjects.</note>.

*A.* You tell of wonders! As if she did not already have enough covers and disguises <note>original: *pigmentorum*—literally "paints" or "cosmetics," used here to mean the false "coloring" or outward show of a hypocrite.</note> without also shutting herself in a fortress.

*B.* She was warned by "faithful" men that something was being <unclear>scented</unclear> out and that there was a general ill-will; therefore, she needs some secure hideaway.

*A.* Who are those "faithful" ones?

*B.* Bah! Why do you ask? They are those who profess the secrets of empires, by which a bridle is put on the common people and chaff is thrown before them; those who feign a trade with heaven, by whom the common folk are cast down and reverence is squeezed out; those who play at literary deceptions <note>original: *literarū præstigias*—the use of scholarly or sophisticated language to trick or "dazzle" the unlearned.</note>, by which the crowd is enticed and subjected to vanity.

*A.* It appears you are some sort of secretary, you speak so obscurely.

*B.* Well then, name for me some more famous Architect whom I might consult.

*A.* Vitruvius, Marlianus, Frontinus, Serlio, Specklin, Lorini, Perret, Stevin, the Fleming, Schickard, Bramer <note>A prestigious list of architectural and engineering authorities. It spans from the ancient Romans Vitruvius and Frontinus to Renaissance masters like Serlio and contemporary 17th-century engineers like the German Schickard and the Dutchman Simon Stevin.</note>.

*B.* Does Hypocrisy not abhor every one of these?

*A.* Then consult Tiberius Caesar, or Caesar Borgia, or Ferdinand of Aragon <note>Three historical figures who were archetypes of political cunning and "reason of state" in the early modern imagination.</note>.

*B.* It is not permitted to approach such great lords.

*A.* Rejoice, for a man has come to my mind who could supply a thousand hiding places; indeed, he can stand in for them all. Some hooded Prior, with a shaven beard, a bald crown, a pale face, and a hanging head...

## 82. THE GOSPEL.

*A.* "Woe to me, my mother, that you gave birth to me, a man of discord in all the earth! I have neither lent money, nor has anyone lent to me, yet everyone curses me." <note>This is a direct paraphrase of the biblical prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 15:10), used here to express the exhaustion of someone whose commitment to truth brings only conflict.</note>

*B.* Who is lamenting here?

*A.* It is I, your friend, whom you know to be afflicted on all sides.

*B.* What? Have you not yet moved your Patrons to take up the defense <note>original: *patrocinium*—legal or formal protection provided by a powerful social superior to a subordinate.</note> of your reputation and innocence?

*A.* On the contrary, they only grow more hardened.

*B.* And that in a matter so clear!

*A.* It is not permitted to defend an innocent man when a powerful person <note>original: *formidabilis*—someone who is "formidable" or feared because of their power.</note> is offended.

*B.* And yet your judges are usually warned not to show partiality to any person.

*A.* Do you not know that some sacrifice to Satan <note>original: *Sathanæ sacrificare*—a cynical proverb or metaphor about appeasing a dangerous person or power purely to prevent harm, rather than out of genuine devotion.</note> not so that he might help them, but so that he might not hurt them?

*B.* It appears that is happening here too: for the one they truly hate, they greet with smooth words and wish to call a friend. But what hope remains?

*A.* Patience—which death perhaps will end. For why should I live on, sad in spirit, sick in body, stripped of my goods, and wounded in my reputation?

# THE DONKEY.

In French: "The oxen" (says Montanus <note>Referring to Michel de Montaigne, who recounts this story in his *Essays*, Book II, Chapter 12.</note>) "which served in the Royal gardens of Susa <note>An ancient capital of the Persian Empire.</note> to water them and turn certain large wheels for drawing water, to which buckets are attached: they were ordered to draw up to a hundred turns each per day. They were so accustomed to this number that it was impossible by any force to make them draw a single turn more; and having finished their task, they stopped short." <note>original French: *Les boeufs... qui servoyent aux iardins Royaux de Suse...*</note> Look how much wiser these oxen are than many men, who are led even to death by the slightest persuasion. And so this shall be the rule: that only the Christian uses his reason well, and especially in this time; the rest are either worse or more wretched than beasts.

### 86. PARADOXES.

**A.** Can you bear to have any companion in your studies? 

**B.** Indeed, I would want a whole crowd of them, but I do not know why my **paradoxes** <note>In the Renaissance, "paradoxes" were a popular literary genre—statements that seemed absurd or contradictory but were intended to reveal a deeper, often spiritual, truth.</note> seem wise to no one. 

**A.** Perhaps you are disliked because you strive for obscurity. 

**B.** On the contrary, nothing is plainer, simpler, or shorter. 

**A.** Could you explain yourself to me over the space of a few days? 

**B.** Certainly in two or three minutes. 

**A.** O, let me hear it from you then. 

**B.** I owe you that much; I only wish you would admit it to be true. 

**A.** Hurry, then: for minutes flow away quickly. 

**B.** Know that **God** is this very thing which He commands. God meets the one who turns back <note>original: *repenti*—likely referring to one who repents or turns back toward the right path.</note>, but He flees the one who pursues Him. God, even when seen from afar, is near. God often delivers one from sin through sin itself; the name of God is the covering <note>original: *oper-* likely *operculum* or *operimentum*. ### PARADOXES.

## 87. THE POLYMATH <note>original: *Polimathes*—A person of wide-ranging knowledge or learning.</note>

A. Throw away the book. B. I would prefer gold. A. At least put it down for a friend’s sake. B. I do so with reluctance, for no one is a better friend than a good little book. A. ->### THE POLYMATH <note>original: *Polimathes*—A person of wide-ranging knowledge or learning.</note><-

do you thrust forward something meager, or copied from elsewhere, or plucked away from its source? *A.* Spare our learned men. *B.* Come now, I will not even set against you Turnebus <note>Adrien Turnèbe (1512–1565), a French classical scholar and chair of Greek at the Collège Royal.</note>, Zwinger <note>Theodor Zwinger (1533–1588), author of the massive encyclopedia *Theatrum Humanae Vitae*.</note>, or Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), often considered the greatest scholar of the Renaissance.</note>; instead, I will oppose you with the *Universal Library* <note>original: *Bibliotheca*—referring to Conrad Gessner's *Bibliotheca Universalis* (1545), the first universal bibliography.</note> and the *Pandects* <note>original: *Pandectas*—Gessner's subject-indexed supplement to his bibliography.</note> of Conrad Gessner alone. Or rather, who would believe it? *B.* And so, would it not be praiseworthy for many people to collect some excellent and most rare work under the direction and method of a single person? They betray themselves by an incongruous and uneven patching together of things, and they prostitute themselves by showing how little they understand of the works of others. For it is a shameful thing to wish to seem to have constructed a house when one has stolen the windows, the locks, the hinges, the arches, the boards, the jars, and the roof tiles. *A.* Thus, it is most advisable for each person to practice the art which he has actually learned. *B.* But it is also a mark of the highest genius to employ many craftsmen for one excellent work. *A.* I could easily name quite a few such men among us today. *B.* Such men indeed—to tell you the truth—who wish to seem to the unskilled to understand many and varied things, but are caught being ignorant of their own subjects when faced by individual craftsmen.

## 88. DEFINITIONS.

**A.** Why are you scratching your ears and tugging at your temples? <note>These physical gestures traditionally signaled deep concentration or intellectual frustration.</note> **B.** I am meditating. **A.** You usually are, but are you giving birth to anything serious? ## 90. BVTTVBATTA.

<margin>B.</margin> Hey there, mortals! All of you who marvel at unheard-of arts, who peer into the supernatural, who exhaust your wits with subtleties, who squander your wealth on the world’s rarest wonders: come here! Gather ‘round! Behold new treasures, new and incredible gifts from heaven. See how generous, easy, and ready I am—for free, for free, for free, whatever is here shall be given! Hurry to me!

**A.** What is this shouting and bold talk?

**B.** Come here, good man, and share these riches with me.

**A.** You are going to distribute riches, dressed in that torn little cloak, boots full of holes <note>original: *fenestratis caligis*, literally "windowed boots," meaning boots worn through with holes</note>, and a threadbare shirt?

**B.** I say treasures, riches, gems, and all things fit for a king.

**A.** Come now, name your crumbs, your scraps, your little labels, your filthy rags.

**B.** You laugh, but I will show you the art of finding all treasures and every art; then I shall display an unquenchable torch and an oil that is never consumed. <note>These refer to "ever-burning lamps," a common legend in alchemy and archaeology of the time.</note> I will place flexible glass <note>original: *vitrum ductile*. This refers to a famous Roman legend of glass that could be bent or dented without breaking; the inventor was supposedly executed by Tiberius to protect the value of gold.</note> into your hands and teach you how to extract the essence of power from all growing things. Then I shall establish a way to converse with animals and extend life beyond the years of Nestor. <note>Nestor was a legendary Greek hero known for his great age and wisdom, said to have lived through three generations.</note> If you wish to fly, I will fit you with wings; if you wish to move the earth, I will provide the machines.

**A.** You wicked man! Have you no shame in lying so boldly? Watch out, for your shouting will soon lead you to chains.

**B.** I would even suffer my head to be cut off if I do not prove every single thing right here and now.

**A.** You continue to lie.

**B.** Come now, if you—a learned man—acknowledge these things through me, will you give me a modest payment for my travels? <note>original: *viaticum*, referring to money or supplies given for a journey.</note>

**A.** I will give...

### 92. THE HORN OF PLENTY.

**A.** Why do you sigh, oh friend? **B.** Do you not see the commonwealth being ruined by the works of both the princes and the leading men? **A.** Is there something you find lacking in them? **B.** Much, and many things. **A.** If you had a <term>Horn of Plenty</term> <note>original: *copiae cornu*, or Cornucopia; a mythological symbol of abundance and unlimited gifts.</note>, what above all would you grant them? **B.** To each I would add something, and from each I would take something away. **A.** Tell me, what for the Princes? **B.** Ten times more religion, and I would take away from their extravagance. **A.** What for the Councilors? **B.** I would wish them more courage, and less private interest. **A.** What for the <term>Consistory</term> <note>original: *Consistorio*. This is a play on the Latin idiom for someone who cannot keep a secret or who is full of flaws.</note>

-># THE HORN OF PLENTY<-

**A.** What for the nobles? **B.** More courage, less pride.
**A.** What for the courtiers? **B.** More restraint, less worldliness. <note>original: *prophanitatis*. This refers to a lack of sacred or serious purpose; a focus on the secular and trivial.</note>
**A.** What for the theologians? **B.** More of the [good] example, less ambition.
**A.** What for the legal experts? **B.** More conscience, less [desire for] profit.
**A.** What for the physicians? **B.** More experience, less envy.
**A.** What for the professors? **B.** More brains, less arrogance. <note>original: *supercilii*, literally "eyebrow," referring to the haughty expression of one who looks down on others.</note>
**A.** What for the schoolmasters? **B.** More substance, less Scholasticism. <note>Scholasticism here refers to a rigid, overly-complex method of teaching and logic that the author views as outdated or pedantic.</note>
**A.** What for the politicians? **B.** More integrity, less atheism.
**A.** What for the historians? **B.** More prudence, less fables.
**A.** What for the ethicists? **B.** More Christianity, less of the pagans. <note>A critique of moral philosophers who rely too heavily on ancient Greek and Roman thinkers rather than Christian scripture.</note>

# THE MISER. 1.

**R.** You have said it well: these times are troublesome and most difficult, and it is not easy to stay afloat <note>original: *emergere*, literally "to emerge" or "to rise up." When the need arises—which is rare—I do not run to the merchant immediately; instead, I check the second-hand market <note>original: *scrutarium forum*, a marketplace for old clothes, scraps, or discarded goods.</note> or see if it is being sold at auction. **H.** And do you get it for less? **R.** Absolutely. Buyers must be sought, debtors pressured, workmen watched; I must see if fortune might smile from any direction. **H.** And what of God? **R.** All these things come from Him: the impulse, the blessing, the multiplication, and the preservation. Whatever I own, through my labors...

Dogs, birds, and exotic beasts should not be fed unless they are useful; food should be taken only once a day; the household staff should not drink wine, nor should they fall in love; clothes should be made of nothing but leather; and gamblers, thieves, tax collectors, and beggars—all should perish. **H.** What if you die before you see these things? **R.** Always death, death! While we live, let us live, lest by our own fault we fall into the hands of others. This is our portion which God has given: to diminish it is a crime, to keep it the same is inglorious, but to increase it is at once most pleasant and most useful. **H.** "He has won every vote who has joined the useful with the sweet" <note>original: *Omne tulit punctum qui miscuit utile dulci*, a famous quote from Horace's *Ars Poetica* meaning that the best approach combines pleasure with utility.</note>. **R.** Truly, truly; but I have been away from my house too long. If these keys did not comfort me, I would fear the ruin of my household. **H.** Not...

# THE QUARRELER. 3.
## CREMES, WIFE, HERACLITUS.

**C.** Get out, you wicked woman, poisoner, sacrilegious wretch, adulteress!
**W.** Bah, you scoundrel! You will vomit up your soul sooner than you will prove these things.
**C.** Why are you babbling, you harlot?
**W.** Why are you striking me, you disgrace?
**C.** This is what is given to a woman who loves "men" but not "her man" <note>A pun on the Latin *viros* (men) and *virum* (husband/man).</note>.
**W.** You lie, you villain!
**C.** Take that!
**W.** Woe is me! You bandit, thief, plunderer, adulterer, traitor, parricide, sorcerer, pimp, sodomite!
**C.** Bah, the tongue of a woman! Take more of a beating.
**W.** Shall I die unavenged, you triple-thief <note>original: *trifurcifer*; a comic Roman term for a consummate scoundrel.</note>, glutton, gambler, bastard, runaway? Take that!
**C.** Take that, you hag.
**W.** Take that, you fool, madman, simpleton, driver of crimes!
**C.** Take that, you whore.
**W.** Take that, you beast, brute, ass, pig, ox, capon <note>original: *capo*; a castrated rooster, used here as a stinging insult to his masculinity.</note>, appendix of the brothel!
**C.** May God destroy you!
**W.** May the Devil tear you apart!
**C.** May the earth gape open for you!
**W.** May the mountains crush you!
**C.** May the water choke you!
**W.** May the fire consume you!
**C.** May the plague slaughter you!
**W.** May the itch, leprosy, wasting disease, colic, rot, lice, and the French disease <note>original: *Gallicus morbus*; a common historical term for syphilis.</note> consume you all together!
**C.** There, take a most hard beating!
**W.** O you most ruined oath-breaker!
**C.** You most worthless of all!
**W.** Be cursed for eternity!
**C.** I am doing nothing unless I kill you.
**W.** O citizens, citizens! O you bandit—

You make the life that nature has imposed as a miserable thing even more miserable for yourself; and the hours which ought to be devoted to your lamentable imperfections, you instead bestow upon quarrels and curses. **V.** <note>Abbreviation for *Uxor*, the wife.</note> What is this man babbling about? **C.** I do not know, except that I believe him to be insane. **H.** <note>Heraclitus, the "weeping philosopher."</note> I beg you, answer me something. **C.** Gladly, for I think you will be quite ridiculous. **H.** Whoever I may be, tell me: did you marry this wife long ago, or recently? **C.** I wish it were recently. **V.** Bah! Too long ago? **C.** I wish it were never. **H.** Are quarrels rare between you, or very frequent? **C.** Very frequent. **H.** But do reconciliations intervene, or are you angry perpetually? **C.** There are some, but they are like nights in summer. <note>A metaphor meaning the peace is very brief, just as summer nights are the shortest of the year.</note> **H.** Furthermore, when you are reconciled, do you acknowledge your errors, or confess to one another and improve for the future? For you ought to finally grasp the cause of the disagreement. **C.** Bah, you fool! The causes are daily and spontaneous. **H.** How so? **V.** Why do you even listen to him, my husband? Let us go to lunch. **C.** Let us go indeed, but it would have been better to do so long ago. **V.** So be it, because so it was. **H.** Immortal God, what shall I say? What is this? Do I dream or am I awake? To be angry, to curse, to strike, to reproach, to be reconciled, to love, to laugh—and not even know why! Ah, hateful life, how you press and weigh down those foul actors of the play, and me, the unhappy spectator. Alas, alas, alas. <note>original: *heu heu heu*; Heraclitus concludes the scene by viewing the human condition as a senseless theatrical performance.</note>

<term>quarreler</term> <note>original: *litigator*; one who habitually disputes or takes part in legal or verbal strife.</note>, <term>quarrels</term> <note>original: *iurgia*; specifically verbal altercations or brawls.</note>, <term>reconciliation</term>, <term>spouse</term>, <term>lunch</term> <note>original: *prandium*; the midday meal.</note>, <term>discord</term> <note>original: *dissidium*; a falling out or separation of minds.</note>

### THE CARELESS MAN. Scene 4. VULCAN, DEMOCRITUS.

**D.** <note>Democritus, the ancient Greek philosopher known for laughing at the follies of mankind.</note> Come forth again, Democritus, so that you may have something to laugh at: for as this place is prepared for madness, material for laughter will never be lacking today. Indeed, if you were to look only at his misery, the man is not to be laughed at but rather pitied; yet to look at his foolishness—a task I have taken upon myself from among the great number of spectators—is so utterly ridiculous that you would marvel that anything could be so laughable. They court misery, and within it they gesticulate so variedly and so foolishly, and meanwhile they laugh at one another, so that it seems to me even inanimate objects would want to laugh at them. But who is this? Ha! That "horned" one <note>A historical reference to a cuckold; it was a common joke that a husband whose wife was unfaithful would grow invisible horns.</note>, that cuckoo <note>original: *cuculus*; a term for a man whose wife is unfaithful, derived from the bird that lays eggs in other birds' nests.</note>, that husband of another man’s wife, that father of other men's children, a servant in his own home. Let us listen to him.

**V.** <note>Vulcan, the blacksmith god, famously portrayed in mythology as the husband of the unfaithful Venus.</note> How troublesome it is for me that my wife is away for so long, and I cannot enjoy her sweet conversation, her delightful kisses, and her tender embraces.

**D.** Ha, ha, he!

**V.** But she is now anxious for my sake, and is running about everywhere so that she may provide for me and the household.

**D.** Enough indeed with the burden of her belly. <note>Democritus implies she is pregnant by another man.</note>

**V.** How blessed it is to have a chaste wife, who loves her husband and is useful to the family; and then to have children who resemble their parents, who are obedient and most beautiful.

**D.** It is only right to have beautiful children, since they are fathered by the most beautiful men chosen from all over. <note>A sarcastic comment suggesting the children are not Vulcan's.</note>

**V.** Who is speaking here? Ah, it is that most festive Democritus.

**D.** What is happening, what is happening, Vulcan?

**V.** Here one walks, one rejoices, one waits.

**D.** Whom are you waiting for?

**V.** Why do you ask? For her who hastens home, who [longs for] her husband's meeting...

# THE FOOL 6.

## BURATIN, DEMO-
## CRITUS.

**B.** Greetings, citizens! I do not know what my soul foretells, but I feel this day will be a holiday for us, and most clearly ours. When I was inside just now, I saw everything was full of fools; therefore I have come out to see if perhaps there might even be someone here who could adorn our order. Come, let us look around. Bah! Either I clearly see nothing, or I discern poorly—there are so many here! But keep quiet, please, Buratin (for that is my name): they do not want to be named, and while they are most in the public eye, they wish to be invisible. It is enough; I have something to tell you. I should have come forward a long time ago to recite a charming story <note>original: *historiam lepidam*.</note> to you, but I had not yet learned it well enough, and my boots <note>original: *caligae*; heavy boots often worn by soldiers or travelers.</note> were not fitted quite right, and some others got ahead of me—it is a wonder they were able to do it without me. However, there is no danger, for whatever was done before me will be made obsolete, and has already been set aside by the New Decree <note>original: *Novellam*; likely a pun on the *Novellae Constitutiones* (new laws) of Roman law and a "novelty" or new story.</note>. Now, hear what I want from you. ## SCENE 7
### HUBERTUS, HERACLITUS,
### THE CITY MINISTER.

**Hb.** Bah, how troublesome and dangerous it is to rule! No one would lift crowns from the dung <note>original: *stercore*; manure or filth. ## THE COUNSELOR. 9.

### GRATIANVS, HERACLITVS, BVRATIN.

**GRATIANVS.** How wretched it is that those who rule do not know how to rule, while those who serve know how to rule! Meanwhile, our affairs are thrown into confusion and almost depend entirely on Fortune! This age, full of letters, full of arts, and most full of novelties, always makes itself more difficult for its own people! *H.* <note>Heraclitus, the "weeping philosopher," known for his melancholy view of the world’s constant change.</note> By what good fate have I happened upon a man whom that confused mess of affairs displeases no less than it does me! *G.* Clearly, it is because we exclude reason and depend entirely either on customs or the laws of our fathers. Or, because we—either ignorant or silent and beholden to private profit <note>original: *privato lucello* — a diminutive term for petty or shameful gain</note>—allow the vices of states to enter. What else should we fear than a revolution <note>original: *immutatio* — literally a changing or alteration of the state's foundations</note> of the Republic? What else but some remarkable upheaval is to be expected? *H.* It appears this man sees our encroaching evils; but let us chat instead. *G.* This man is heading straight for me; it would be a wonder if he does not ask for a promotion or some intercession. *H.* May God grant you what [you wish]. <note>The sentence concludes on the following page.</note>

## COMPLAINT II
## ON HUMAN LIFE.

# FANTASY AND SORROW.

# COMPLAINTS ON HUMAN LIFE
### THE VANITY OF PHILOSOPHY
#### A Dialogue between Phantasia and Tristis

->228<-

...which outside of himself no one sees, no one recognizes, no one desires, no one believes, and no one praises; they are frivolous and ridiculous things of that sort, by which our life is consumed somewhat more unhappily than the lives of the most wretched—that is, in a vain fulfillment and agitation of vanity <note>A reference to the Biblical "vanity of vanities" from Ecclesiastes, suggesting a life spent on empty intellectual pursuits</note>.

***P.*** I repeat it again: if you had desired those things which are placed in the hands of everyone, you would have strayed in no way.

***T.*** What things are those?

***P.*** First, to adapt everything to that place where you were born; to observe its customs, laws, and traditions exactly; to praise them sincerely, and to defend them bravely. To grasp the ordinary and solemn methods of rising in status, and to follow those who go before you. To serve **Patrons** <note>In the early modern period, a 'Patronus' was a powerful protector who provided financial support and social advancement in exchange for loyalty</note>, to be at their side, and to make use of them everywhere. To shape your youth according to the ideal and example of those in charge, to mirror them, and with whatever diligence necessary, to make them favorable to you. 

To embrace their opinions and judgments: to doubt nothing, to believe everything; to judge nothing for yourself, to accept all; to find fault with nothing, and to admire everything. This is true simplicity, which finds **Promoters** <note>original: "Promotores"; those who assist in one's social or academic advancement</note> everywhere. It is the level path that leads to the heights, the most secure reasoning that frees one from restlessness, and the easiest method of all. Without dangerous detours, it fully instructs a person far from the dangers of curiosity and the exhaustion of the intellect; it fits one most happily for the uses of society, and most certainly restores one to peace and tranquility. 

But others, who, relying on the arrogance of their own intellect, always want to be their own patrons, their own teachers, their own explainers, and their own defenders—after infinite errors, inexplicable labors, and various dangers, [they find only] mon- <note>The word is cut off by the catchword "ſtroſa", likely completing "monstrosa" or "monstrous things"</note>

<summary>Phantasia argues that intellectual independence leads to misery and social isolation, recommending instead a path of absolute social conformity, obedience to patrons, and the suppression of critical judgment as the only way to achieve peace and success.</summary>

...providence in **paradoxical shifts** <note>original: "strofa paradoxa"; referring to logical turns or life-changes that defy common sense</note>, whirlwinds of the brain, wounds of the conscience, nausea of the mind, debility of the body, hatred of men, and a wild, useless, and troublesome repentance; they are a destruction to themselves and an example to others. 

***T.*** 7. Ah, how easy it is to insult the wretched! Indeed, if there were those who could lead the way candidly, constantly, and truly, and who could manage natural talents with judgment, not only many, but in my opinion the entire world would be better off, and then indeed I would praise your accusation. 

But if those things which are commonly pointed out lead neither to some perfection nor to an elegance of character, nor even bring as much practical use to men as they loudly proclaim, it is no wonder that there are those who try foreign paths. Rather, it is to be grieved that for many, such praiseworthy and tireless efforts become unhappy. 

Just as the torment of temptations compels many to seek **Theologians** <term>scholars of divinity and scripture</term>, and the violence of **Injustice** drives many to seek **Jurists** <term>legal experts and lawyers</term>, and the pain of **Diseases** forces many to seek **physicians**: so also the evils of **ignorance** and **restlessness** do not rest in just one or two people—especially if they employ insufficient means—but they seek help from every side. Yet, this help is as difficult to find as you judge it is to track the path of the inglorious. 

Now I will not say how many of those who have followed their predecessors scrupulously and anxiously in every way have failed to walk happily or reach the goal. Nor will I mention even how minute, trivial, and sometimes unworthy of such leisure or business are the things prescribed, so that they rightly provoke a thirst for movement and action rather than...

...that they might build the summit of sciences and virtues with a more noble intellect. Finally, I will not attack the uncertainty and worthlessness of the arts—about which the practitioners themselves are quite ashamed, and which they hide so much—nor will I even attack their common conspiracy for the sake of feeding their bellies <note>original: "alendi ventris conspirationem"; a cynical reference to professionals who work only for profit rather than truth</note>. For it would be both very difficult to take off such artificial masks and to reject those exquisite and theatrical words of remarkable talkativeness, and dangerous to scatter so many secrets, which are hated by the common people. Let it be enough for me to hope for no better things, not to touch those mystical matters, to avoid human societies everywhere, to be strengthened against any evils, and thus, among so many obstacles of body and soul, to pass an unhappy life.

**P.** I know well you will not stop, if I remain silent, once I have allowed you to break out into your complaints. Certainly, you take this liberty: that after you have wallowed unsuccessfully in everything, and obtained neither an inner taste nor a truer use of individual things, you now attack the outer surfaces of things, and even the husks <note>original: "cortices"; literally the bark or skin of a plant, meaning the superficial appearance</note>. You wish, as if you were exactly skilled in these matters, to deceive <note>original: "fucum facere"; literally to apply makeup or dye to hide a blemish</note> the more ignorant—namely, that by your example, they should neglect titles, honors, riches, literature, and the arts. And you wish that they should instead pursue a life that is solitary, unskillful, stupid, and, if you really want it so, "pious-ish" <note>original: "sanctulum"; a diminutive of saintly, used here derisively to suggest a fake or petty holiness</note>.

**T.** What do you want me to do? Imitate the lives of men? Those who are the harbingers, appraisers, and servants of vanity, turbulence, ambition, anger, and greed? Should I aspire to those studies? They are wagon-loads of doubts, disputes, conflicts, attacks, panegyrics <term>formal speeches of high praise</term>, exaggerations, deceptions, lies, and trifles. Should I enter into a public office? That is a struggle against the ignorance, injustice, malice, and ingratitude of men; a struggle against violence, injury, and the cycles of time; a struggle with weakness, error, shame, and a weariness of one's own self.
