# COMPLAINTS ON HUMAN LIFE
### VIT. HUM. QUER. <note>original: "VIT. HUM. QUER."; abbreviation for Vitae Humanae Querela, or "The Complaint of Human Life"</note>

To seek leisure? Or rather, a lethargy of the soul, a tomb for the body, a fuel for vices, and the rust of virtue. Woe is me, what else should I do? Other than live this daily life, endure daily errors, experience daily misfortunes, and grasp daily goods? I shall use daily things, and in that perpetual change of good and evil, I will not stand immovable—as the wise boast <note>A reference to the Stoic philosophical ideal of remaining emotionally unaffected by external events</note>—but I will be tossed, fluctuate, and float along with it. I am happy now; soon I am sad. Now I am hoping; a little later I am distrusting. I am patient today; tomorrow I am wailing. And just as in the body I am now trembling, now sweating, now pale, now flushing, now running, and soon limping. 

Thus, I think I shall neither reject this earth too much, nor love it too much, but I will keep a mind equal and similar to external evils; a mind which, like a mirror, reflects all days, whether black or white <note>original: "atros, sive albos dies"; a Roman idiom where "white" days were lucky or celebratory and "black" days were unlucky or mournful</note>. Perhaps through this accommodation, the mind will fare better than it would under the imaginary yoke of "wisdom." 

*P.* There are two points on which you are remarkably mistaken. One: that you suggest you have tried all ways of living well. The other: that you do not strive to win people over to yourself even through the smallest and most customary social duties. For if the first <note>meaning a state of comfortable rest and "living well"</note> happened for many people only after the labors of many years, after various tossings of fortune, and after most wretched service—and indeed for most of them only in old age—so that they might live comfortably and rest happily, what will you think of yourself, you who have not even looked upon the malice of fortune from a distance?

### ->VIT. HUM. QUER.<- <note>original: "VIT. HVM. QVER."; abbreviation for *Vitae Humanae Querela* (The Complaint of Human Life)</note>

...they do not see that, while professing humanity <term>humanitatem: the quality of being human or the pursuit of liberal learning</term>, they are the most arrogant of men. While reciting the virtues of Antiquity <term>Antiquitatis: the classical Greek and Roman past</term>, they attack the virtues of today; finally, by dealing in trifles throughout their whole lives, they wish to be considered the most noble, the best, and the most useful of men.

But as for me—if you do not know it—I do not ask what others think of me, or what men may boast about me once I am gone. Instead, I seek only that it may be truly well with me within myself, <margin>Mark Well</margin> or that a path be shown to me by which I might most perfectly accommodate myself to this life, to these times, to these people—and indeed to whatever nature or fortune might plan anywhere. Thus, you send me back in vain to those whom I have so often experienced as both unfaithful and dangerous; to whom I entrust myself no less unwillingly than they receive me—men with swollen brains, grasping hands, hearts of stone, feigned manners, and painted works <note>original: "operibus pictis"; deeds that are merely for show or hypocritical</note>.

*P.* Tell me: if it were permitted for you to fashion a life for yourself by your own will and to choose your friends, do you believe the earth holds such things that would satisfy you? For if you always consult your own restlessness, what will there finally be that cannot be criticized or accused of imperfection?

*T.* I do not know what the earth may have. Certainly, it is a wretched thing that in this "play of the world" <term>mundi fabula: the philosophical concept that life is a theatrical stage where everyone plays a part</term>, all men are masked <term>personatos: from the Latin "persona," meaning a theatrical mask; playing a role rather than being authentic</term>. No one dares to open their internal turmoils and the conflicts of the mind to another; no one fully uncovers their own ignorance and the errors of their soul; no one reveals the desires of their passions, the doubts of reason, the diversity of their opinions, the mutability of their judgment, or the sorrows of life. Thus, the choice <note>original: "electio"; the catchword "ctio" at the bottom of the page indicates the word continues on the next page</note> of a happier life...

# COMPLAINTS ON HUMAN LIFE
### ->COMPLAINTS ON HUMAN LIFE<- <note>original: "VIT. HUM. QUER."; abbreviation for *Vitae Humanae Querela*</note>

Choice is difficult; the selection of friends is nearly impossible. For as long as we do not obtain command over ourselves, knowledge of ourselves, the shaping of ourselves, and an equilibrium against all the obstacles to happiness that befall a man, it is in vain to hope for such things from others or to expect anything solid from them. 

*P.* See what nonsense you speak, how you falter, imploring the help of men while complaining that those same men are unable to help! You are angry at the obstacles to your peace, and yet you wish for no force to be opposed to them! You accuse others of ignorance, yet you do not allow yourself to be taught! You desire security, yet you struggle against the densest whirlwinds! You hold the world in hatred, and yet you crave familiarity with it! You desire to rest, and yet you change your present goods—and even life itself—so many times. 

Do you now long for something beyond the human? Does it grieve you to be a man? Does it grieve you to be mortal, visible, touchable, hungry, thirsty, sleeping, falling ill, and in need? Does it grieve you that everyone does not love you, feel as you do, praise you, refresh you, or instruct you? Does it grieve you not to know all things, not to possess all things, not to see all things, or not to accomplish all things? Does it grieve you that you cannot fly, or swim, or live in the earth or in fire—and whatever other monsters <note>original: "monstra"; in this context, unnatural desires or strange marvels</note> of human curiosity there may be? 

Little man <term>Homuncio: a diminutive, often used in Stoic philosophy to remind the listener of their small place in the universe</term>: if this life displeases you, depart, for it will be permitted to die whenever you wish. But if you choose to endure the common lot of the rest—which is indeed more tolerable for most—as it befits you to do, then steady yourself with patience and the noble comforts of life, rather than torturing yourself with complaints. Indeed, take utility from every single thing, even from evils, which is a ready thing to do.

# COMPLAINTS ON HUMAN LIFE
### ->COMPLAINTS ON HUMAN LIFE<- <note>original: "VIT. HUM. QUER."; abbreviation for *Vitae Humanae Querela*</note>

...and you recognize them as unfaithful. You urge society, yet you do not teach whose society one should seek! What shall I do if, by always seeking, always hoping, always trying, and always learning, I grow old in this way, and die in this way? If all things are in vain, shall I never have the use of this life, never its pleasure? Will nothing but a wretched death end my misery?

*P.* That is for you to see. For my part, it is not within my power to satisfy you, nor is it possible to correct a head so troubled. If neither the world, nor men, nor studies, nor arts, nor politics, nor works, nor life, nor death please you, I certainly have nothing outside this universe to recommend to you.

*T.* Do you desert me thus?

*P.* Indeed.

*T.* Do not, my friend; perhaps there will be something that at last pleases.

*P.* To be sure—something for which neither I nor you yourself will find a name. A world without creatures, time without change <note>original: "vicissitudine"; the natural ebb and flow or turning of events</note>, good without its opposite, truth without doubt, man without vices, a body without diseases.

*T.* I will confess to you, I would rest easy if I did not fear more unhappy things; for already—and this is most wretched—I have not yet begun to live, and these elements of my life are so bitter to me that I am almost withering in the blade <note>original: "in herba"; a metaphor for failing or dying while still young, before reaching maturity or "harvest."</note>.

*P.* There will come a time when you will laugh at these and other things; there will come a time when you will be angry with yourself for having wept over the flower of your fortune and your youth. There will come a time when, with your skin hardened as it were, you will even have a pleasant familiarity with Patience.

*T.* Let happen what must happen, with the good God; perhaps death is nearer than that such fear should be so necessary for me.

*P.* For now, bring forgetfulness to your foolish fear; as for the rest of what you have spoken with me thus far, you shall be accused before Reason <note>original: "apud Rationem"; Reason is personified here as a judicial authority who will judge the validity of Tristis's complaints.</note>.

*T.* Farewell.

*P.* Live.

<header>INSTRUCTION IN MAGIC. 12.</header>

## FOR THE INQUISITIVE.

### THE INQUISITIVE MAN AND THE CHRISTIAN,

*Inquisitive.* Why are you so alone, Christian? *Christian.* That is my habit; yet though I may be alone, I am with myself, and these advisors of mine are with me. *Inquisitive.* Perhaps I disturbed your advisors with my arrival, and they vanished? *Christian.* On the contrary, they are right here: here are Seneca, Tacitus, de Thou <note>original: "Thanus"; refers to the French historian Jacques-Auguste de Thou</note>, Zwinger <note>original: "Zvvingerus"; likely the polymath Theodor Zwinger</note>, Henninges <note>original: "Henningius"; the genealogist Hieronymus Henninges</note>, and Mercator <note>the famous cartographer Gerardus Mercator</note>. Shall I name more for you? *Inquisitive.* That is enough. But truly, what are you doing? *Christian.* Exactly what you see. I have been examining the detailed illustrations <note>original: "Iconographias"</note> of the Tabernacle of Moses, the Ark of Noah, and the Temple of Solomon—just as my friend Montanus <note>Benito Arias Montano, a scholar famous for his architectural studies of Biblical structures</note> has them here—comparing them against the text of the Scripture. *Inquisitive.* What a ridiculous man. What interest is it of yours to know the structure of either the Tabernacle or the Temple? None of these things contribute anything to our religion, except perhaps to reveal your own nature, which is prone toward anything monstrous and unusual. *Christian.* Is it not better to think on these things than to wonder whether a mouse has gnawed a syllable, or whether you yourself are a piece of cheese, or whether you still have that which you never lost? <note>original: "an mus roderit syllabam, an tu esses Caseum, an quod amisiffes, haberes"; these are references to classic "sophisms" or logical puzzles used in university debates that the author considers trivial or silly.</note> and other such "subtleties." But tell me: if our Prince summoned the most excellent architects from every corner of the world and wished them to compete in their art, with the costs most generously covered, would it not be worth our while to go there and inspect the works of each man? Would we not examine every detail most exquisitely, to see by what art this or that...

<term>Magician</term> (Magus) — in the Renaissance, this often referred to a "natural" philosopher who understood the hidden laws of nature, though it carried risks of being accused of witchcraft.
<term>Necromancer</term> (Nigromanticus) — literally "black-diviner," used here to mean someone who commands spirits or demons.
<term>Notary Art</term> (Ars Notoria) — a specific branch of magic focused on acquiring knowledge and memory.
<term>Familiarity of Spirits</term> (Spirituum familiaritas) — the practice of working with "familiar" spirits or servants from the spirit world.
<term>To smelt gold</term> (aurum conflare) — the alchemical goal of creating or purifying gold.

# ### GREAT INSTRUCTION
<note>original: *INST. MAG.* (Institutio Magica)</note>

...another thing, and having conquered so many things in his **imagination**, he added: "Only then shall I finally live sweetly." [His advisor] asked, what was he going to do then? *Cur.* You speak clearly.
*C.* And if you are cast into water, or in a bath, when you are already completely soaked, no matter what is finally poured over you, you cannot become *more* soaked.
*Cur.* That is so.
*C.* Indeed, all the rest flows past your **body** and runs off.
*Cur.* That is true.
*C.* And a man thrown into the sea cannot be drowned any more than in a small tub; one or two cups [of water] do the job.
*Cur.* I grant that.
*C.* And the man upon whom an entire **house** collapses is no more killed than if a single tile had fallen from the roof of the **house**.
*Cur.* That is enough.

*C.* It was drummed into me differently once. He who makes progress in **learning**...

### GREAT INSTRUCTION

**C.** No doubt you are expecting something magical. Tell me instead: if some common person knew that we possessed such a mirror, would they not marvel at us, or envy us this good fortune?
**Cur.** That is indeed their nature.
**C.** Then if, out of pure laziness <note>original: *oscitantia*, literally "yawning" or "drowsiness," implying a mental sluggishness</note>, we were unwilling to look into that Mirror, nor wished to foreknow the outcomes of things, but preferred to wait for them anxiously alongside the common crowd, or be led in our affairs by the errors of others—and the most unskilled others at that—would not anyone who called us "doubly foolish" and "doubly insane" be speaking the truth?

Furthermore, find yourself other companions in this study of yours, so that you may meet and discuss these matters very frequently among yourselves. Keep this one rule: that you always fix your eyes on the goal of use in human conversation, and aim your discussions toward that mark. You cannot help but know how many—indeed, how infinite—are the things we learn with great labor, which nevertheless can never bring any lasting benefit to human interests. Why are they cast aside? Yet these are the very things that, as it were, unlock nature herself to us and make her favorable; furthermore, they provide the best distraction from civil discord and turmoil.

I think the same of the **Mathematicians** <note>In this context, specifically astronomers.</note>, from whom I desire only this: that they exactly display the **phenomena** to me—whether the **earth** moves and the **sun** stands still, or the sun moves and the earth rests, or whether the earth moves from its place or revolves on its own axis—none of which poses any danger to us. For it is not our opinion that will make the sun move or stand still; let it be enough for us to measure time exactly and to sense <note>original: "subodorari" — literally "to catch the scent of."</note> the **harmony** that God has instilled in all things.

IF you have read through these [writings] of mine, prudent reader <note>original: Cordate lector; literally "wise-hearted reader," a common address in Renaissance literature</note>, which are *neither entirely serious, nor altogether playful, I pray that you kindly dismiss them, and do not examine them according to the strict rule <note>original: amussim; a carpenter’s tool used for checking levels, here meaning a rigid or perfectionist standard</note> of your more noble intellect.
